When Space Marines fail a Break Test, they become Shaken instead of Broken. Shaken Space Marines may not move towards the enemy, but can still pivot to face them, Shoot, fight in Hand-to-Hand Combat, and participate in the Psychic Phase. Where every move open to them would close on the enemy—when they are surrounded, for instance—they may not move at all beyond turning to face; otherwise they move freely, into cover or off the table edge.

Shaken Space Marines attempt to Rally as Broken troops do, and shed Shaken status the moment they pass, acting normally from their next turn. Insane Bravery and Craven Cowardice do not apply to them.

Shaken Space Marines engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat may only make a Follow-Up Move to move into Cover or to engage another enemy that is already fighting a Space Marine.

Failing an additional Break Test whilst Shaken causes Space Marines to become Broken.

A drop pod is fired from orbit and comes down under retros that slow it just enough to survive the fall. Only a Space Marine army fields them, and only allies in fully enclosed environment suits may ride down in one.

Landing

Each pod needs a 2" Blast Marker. Number the markers and note what each pod carries before the battle begins. Pods arrive in the Space Marine player's Movement Phase. Place each marker on clear ground anywhere on the table, each within 10" of the marker placed before it.

Roll the Scatter Dice for each pod. A hit brings it down on the marker. An arrow sends it the way the arrow points, over the distance rolled on the chart below.

Drop Pod Scatter Chart (2D6)

2
Something has gone badly wrong. Roll on the Catastrophic Launch Chart.
3-12
The pod comes down that many inches from the marker, in the direction the Scatter Dice gave.

Catastrophic Launch Chart (D6)

1
The heat shield fails and the pod burns up on the way down, with everything in it.
2
The pod bursts on impact, throwing out D6 Strength 10 hits.
3
Fire in the hold. Every model aboard takes a Strength 4 hit at -2, treated as a flamer hit, and may therefore Catch on Fire.
4
Wildly off target. The squad walks on from its own table edge at the start of the next turn.
5
The doors jam, and the occupants must cut their way out.
6
Delayed. Roll on the Drop Pod Scatter Chart again next turn.

A pod that comes down on Impassable Terrain is destroyed. One carried off the table is lost, but the troops it held walk on at the start of the next turn, within 6" of the point where it left. On Very Difficult Terrain roll a D6: on a 1, 2 or 3 the pod tips over and its doors count as jammed, and on a 4 or more the retros clear the ground and it lands square.

An enemy model under the marker may throw itself clear by rolling under its Initiative on a D6, where a 6 always fails, and is then placed against the side of the pod. A vehicle is caught automatically, except a dreadnought, which tests as a model does. Anything that fails to get clear takes a Strength 10 hit causing D20 wounds at -6.

A pod landing on a vehicle is worked out as a Ram, at the pod's own ram value. Only the Armour Value of the pod's underside counts, while the vehicle uses its highest. A vehicle whose armour is beaten is crushed and destroyed, and the pod stays where it is; a pod that fails to beat it lands badly and is left inverted. A building or a Fortification struck this way is treated as a vehicle, while soft cover, trees and Difficult Terrain under a pod are simply destroyed.

Two pods coming down in the same turn land side by side. In later turns one may land on another, and only the arriving pod counts the underside armour.

Opening

The pod's sides fall outward when its locking bolts fire, though re-entry may have fused them shut. Roll a D6: on a 2 or more the pod opens, and on a 1 it stays shut until the following turn, when it may be tried again.

Doors jammed by damage, by re-entry or by the pod landing inverted open only on a D6 roll of 4 or more, and only one attempt is ever allowed. A failure seals them for good, and they must be broken open instead.

Troops may not leave the pod in the turn it lands, though they may shoot as normal. Once the doors are open they move and fight as usual, and a Support Weapon aboard fires in the Shooting Phase.

Assault Pods

An assault pod carries ten Space Marines whatever armour they wear, so either a squad or two combat squads. A pod carrying a Wolf Lord, a Space Marine Captain or a Commander adds 1 to its roll on the Drop Pod Scatter Chart.

Marines in an assault pod that is inverted or jammed may cut their way out with close combat weapons, fighting the pod as a vehicle in Hand-to-Hand Combat and rolling for Armour Penetration as usual. A penetration cuts an opening rather than damaging the pod, and no damage roll is made; the models inside move clear in the following turn at half their Movement.

An empty assault pod is worth no Victory Points at all, even under Engage and Destroy. One destroyed with its Marines still aboard scores as a vehicle does.

Support Pods

A support pod carries no crew, only a turret-mounted Heavy Plasma Gun on an autofire targeter. It fires from the turn the pod opens, choosing targets under the normal rules at Ballistic Skill 4, and the targeter limits it to 24" whatever the weapon would otherwise reach.

Support pods are bought only alongside assault pods, one for every two assault pods, rounding up. A support pod is worth 1 Victory Point to the enemy, and another under Engage and Destroy.

Deathwind Pods

A deathwind pod carries a missile launcher that trips as the pod opens and turns, throwing missiles in every direction. It fires in the Shooting Phase of the turn the doors open. Every model within 10" is hit on a D6 roll of 4 or more, whatever its cover and whatever it did that turn, taking a Strength 4 hit of 1 wound at -1. The missiles count as a blast weapon where flak armour is concerned.

The launcher fires once and once only, after which the pod does nothing further but stand as cover. A deathwind pod that has fired is worth no Victory Points; one destroyed before it fires scores as a support pod does.

There are numerous types of armour in the 41st millennium, ranging from the humble Flak jacket up to the almost impenetrable bulwark of Tactical Dreadnought Armour. If a model wearing armour is hit by a close combat or ranged weapon, an armour saving throw is made. If the model passes the save, no damage is taken. To pass an armour save, the dice roll must be greater than or equal to the Armour Save value.

Save Modifiers

Some weapons are powerful enough to negate part, or even all, of an armour's protection; this is represented by a Save Modifier on the weapon's profile. For example, if a model is wearing Mesh armour with a base save value of 5+, and it is hit by a Boltgun that has a save modifier of -1, the modified roll becomes 6+. If the modified save is greater than the highest possible dice score, then the armour is automatically penetrated.

An obstacle up to 1" high and/or 1" broad is crossed without penalty. One taller than that, up to twice the height of the model crossing it, takes half the model's Movement to cross. Anything higher than twice the model's own height counts as Impassable Terrain for that model.

A model without enough Movement left to cross an obstacle halts in front of it. No model is ever left standing half way across.

If an obstacle has a gate, the gate is assumed to be open unless otherwise agreed, and troops may pass through as if it were open terrain.

The penalties for Difficult Terrain types and obstacles are cumulative.

For every pair of opposing models in base-to-base contact, a Combat Round is resolved by the following steps:

  1. Roll Attack Dice

    Each player rolls a number of D6 equal to their model's Attacks characteristic. If they have two or more weapons with the Close Combat rule, they add 1 D6 to their roll.

  2. Calculate Combat Score

    Each player picks their single highest scoring dice and adds the result to the model's Weapon Skill. They then apply Combat Score Modifiers to this total to determine their Combat Score.

  3. Determine the Winner

    The model with the highest Combat Score is declared the winner of the Combat Round. The winner scores a number of hits equal to the difference between Combat Scores. If Combat Scores are tied, the model with the highest Initiative wins and scores a single hit. If Initiative is also tied, the Combat Round is a stalemate and no hits are scored.

  4. Resolve Hits & Damage

    The losing model sustains the number of hits scored by the winner. For each hit, Damage and Armour Saves are worked out as normal. When resolving damage, each hit is struck at the higher of the winner's own Strength and that of any Close Combat weapon they carry. The hit also takes the greater Save Modifier of weapon and wielder.

First and foremost, 2nd Edition 40k is meant to be fun. The rules should serve the story you want to tell on the tabletop, not dictate it. Remember, the ultimate goal is a memorable, immersive battle that leaves everyone eager for the next game. Be a good sport and have fun!

Warhammer 40,000 is a challenging and involving game, with many fantastic races, and endless possibilities. In a game of this size and level of complexity there are bound to be some situations where the rules seem unclear, or a particular situation lies outside the rules as they are written. This is inevitable, as we can't possibly give rules to cover every circumstance. Nor would we want to try, as that would restrict what you can and cannot do far too much. Players should feel free to invent and improvise, exploring the galaxy of Warhammer 40,000 for themselves and taking the game far beyond the published rules if they wish.

—Rick Priestley & Andy Chambers, Warhammer 40,000 Rulebook (2nd Edition)

Force weapons may only be wielded by psykers, and take many shapes; rods, axes and swords are the ones most often seen.

In Hand-to-Hand Combat the weapon adds the psyker's Mastery Level to their Strength for the roll to wound. That same number worsens the Save Modifier of the hit. Where the weapon's profile carries a Strength of its own, the higher of the two applies†.

† The base rulebook gives only the mastery-level bonus; the higher-of-the-two clause comes from the force weapon entries in the Wargear book.

A Space Marine Chief Librarian at Mastery Level 4 and Strength 5, holding a Force Sword, therefore strikes at Strength 9 with a Save Modifier of -6.

A daemon struck in Hand-to-Hand Combat by a force weapon is wounded outright, with no roll to wound made at all. The daemonic saving throw, which nothing else modifies, counts for nothing against a force weapon.

Shoot at a vehicle as at any other model, using true Line of Sight. Most obstacles and low cover do not block line of sight to or from a vehicle.

A vehicle may claim Cover as troops do, but at least a third of it must be obscured to do so. Some vehicles count as a Large Target, and a vehicle counts as a Fast Moving Target or Very Fast Moving Target according to the distance it moved in its own turn. All apply as Basic To Hit Modifiers.

Sustained Fire works against a vehicle exactly as it does against troops.

For each hit, roll a D6 on the hit location table on the back of the vehicle's Datafax. Where a location cannot be hit from the firer's position, re-roll until a location that can be hit is indicated.

Hits From Blast Markers

A weapon using a Blast Marker treats each location on the vehicle as a separate target. Roll to hit, and Scatter on a miss, as normal. The location that completely fills the hole at the centre of the marker is hit automatically; every other location covered or partly covered is hit on a D6 roll of 4+. Roll Armour Penetration separately against each location hit.

A game of Warhammer 40,000 2nd Edition can be broken down into a series of steps. This section provides a basic overview of the flow of a game. New players should start here to get a step-by-step picture of a typical game.

An attack that hits a vehicle must penetrate its armour to have any effect.

Armour Value

Every location on a vehicle has an Armour Value, given on the back of its Datafax. The higher the value, the thicker the armour and the harder it is to penetrate.

Front, Side & Rear Shots

A shot fired from within the vehicle's forward 90° arc counts against its front armour. A shot fired from anywhere else counts against its side/rear armour, which on most vehicles is the thinner of the two.

Penetration Tests

Roll a D6 and add the Strength of the weapon that caused the hit. Where the weapon causes a variable amount of damage, roll those dice as well and add them. The total is the thickness of armour penetrated: equal to or greater than the location's Armour Value and the attack penetrates; less and it bounces off, with no further effect. Each weapon's penetration is recorded on its entry under Weapons.

Range

Every full 24" between firer and target strips 1 point from the attack's penetration.

Range Chart

Below 24"
No modifier.
24-48"
Penetration is reduced by 1.
48-72"
Penetration is reduced by 2.
72"+
Penetration is reduced by 3.

Bonus Penetration Dice

Hand-to-hand attacks and psychic attacks add the dice below to the penetration total, according to the Strength of the attack. Shooting earns no such bonus.

Bonus Penetration Dice Chart (Attack Strength)

1-3
No bonus.
4-5
Add 1D6.
6-7

Add 1D20.

The Movement Phase is comprised of four steps that are followed in strict order:

  1. Declare Charges

    Any charge into Hand-to-Hand Combat must be declared before any units are moved or measuring takes place.

  2. Compulsory Moves

    Move any units that are subject to a compulsory movement rule—such as vehicles moving out of control.

  3. Move Chargers

    Move any units that were nominated to charge in the first step.

  4. Normal Moves

    Move any other units.

The Heroic Character with the highest Leadership is designated as the army's Commander. If more than one Heroic Character has the same Leadership, the player nominates one to be the Commander.

Any unit within 12" of the Commander may use the Commander's Leadership value instead of its own when making any Leadership Tests.

If the Commander is slain, any units within 12" must take an immediate Break Test, even if they have already taken one in that turn.

The Battle Standard

A Commander may be accompanied by a character bearing the army's battle standard, a rallying point for the whole force and the focus of its pride and determination. The standard need not stay with the Commander, though it serves best nearby. A Heroic Character normally carries it, and every rule for character models applies to the bearer.

Any unit within 12" of the battle standard may retake one failed Break Test a turn. Where the Commander stands within 12" as well, the unit has both that retake and the Commander's Leadership, and will tend to hold its ground whatever comes against it.

The rulebook offers a second choice—a character carrying the Commander's personal banner in place of the army's standard—but gives it no rules of its own, and no published army list offers one. Personal banners survive in the codexes as heraldry alone. Every standard bearer in print, from the Space Marine Company Standard to the Ork Battle Standard, carries the army's battle standard and uses the rules above.

1. Agree on Points

    In Warhammer 40,000, each unit, model, or item is worth a certain number of points—representative of its relative impact on the table. Armies are built by spending points up to an agreed maximum. This is referred to as the Game Size.

    Games can be any size, from small skirmishes up to sprawling mass battles. Some recommended games sizes are:

    • Skirmish - 600 points
    • Standard - 1500 points
    • Large - 2000 points

  2. Select Armies

    To put together an army, points are spent on units and wargear from one or more army lists. Army lists detail which units and equipment are available when constructing a given force—and how many points they cost—as well as any army specific rules and/or constraints.

    Although it is not a requirement to spend every single point, it is advisable to try to use as many points as possible—wargear can help with this.

  3. Decide Game Length

    4 turns is considered the "default" length for a game; however, players can agree to alter this as they see fit—extending on a turn-by-turn basis until there is a clear winner, ending it prematurely if it is a foregone conclusion, or playing until an agreed time. Some missions or scenarios may also dictate a specific game length.

    A game may instead be played to sudden death, ending the moment either side reaches an agreed total of Victory Points. Or the length may be left to the dice, rolled once before the game begins.

    Game Length Chart (D6)

    1-2
    Three turns.
    3-4
    Four turns.
    5-6
    Five turns.

  4. Mark Deployment Zones

    Deployment Zones are the areas of the game board where each army is placed at the start of the game. Whatever the size of the board, the two zones stand at least 24" apart. Each runs from its own front line all the way back to the table edge behind it, and ends 12" short of the side edges. On the standard 4' x 6' board that gives a zone 12" deep along each long edge, as below.

    In practice, Deployment Zones can be placed anywhere on the game table that serves the narrative of the scenario being played. To draw a Deployment Zone, place markers at each corner—or in a manner that clearly marks its boundary.

    Battle Zone

    Ground that is not a deployment zone is the Battle Zone, marked on the diagram above. Terrain placement and Infiltration are both governed by it.

  5. Place Terrain

    During this step, players construct the battlefield for the game. Both players roll a D6, and the higher score places the first piece of terrain; they then alternate. Once one player stops placing, the other may put down a single further piece.

    Every second piece a player puts down must stand in the Battle Zone, and neither player may stop while fewer than 2D6 pieces stand there. A piece is one feature of roughly 4" to 6" square—a wood, a ruin, a low hill.

    Players may instead work together towards a board that fits a narrative theme, such as a pitched battle or a last stand. Beyond the minimum above there is no requirement on what kind of terrain is placed, or how much.

  6. Decide Objectives

    In the simplest game of Warhammer 40,000, the objective is purely to destroy the opponent's army. To give this more flavour, players can define mission objectives for each army. These can be decided in one of two ways:

    Mission Cards

    Mission cards define one or more objectives and the rewards for accomplishing them. Each player takes one. How they are taken is for the players to settle—dealt at random, chosen, or rolled for.

    Scenarios

    A scenario is a narrative through-line for a game—"capture the space port" or "hold out until reinforcements arrive". A great source of inspiration for this are old White Dwarf battle reports—Last Stand at Glazer's Creek, in White Dwarf 222, is one.

    Win Conditions

    The standard way to win a game of Warhammer 40,000 is to score the most Victory Points; however, for some scenarios it may be preferable to define a specific win condition—escaping from a table edge, surviving for X turns, etc.

  7. Draw Strategy Cards (optional)

    Strategy Cards are drawn at random, one for every full 1,000 points an army consists of.

    See Strategy Cards for the full rules.

  8. Draw Psychic Power Cards (optional)

    If either player's force includes Psykers, Psychic Power Cards are dealt before deployment.

    See Dealing Psychic Powers for the full rules.

  9. Deploy Armies

    Armies can be deployed anywhere within an allocated deployment zone, with two restrictions—squads must start the game within Squad Coherency, and vehicles must be deployed on terrain they are normally able to move over. Any model deployed in or behind cover that would conceal it may begin the game in Hiding, marked as hidden in the usual way.

    Both players roll a D6, and the higher score picks which deployment zone to use. The faction with the lowest Strategy Rating always deploys first. Armies formed of allies from different factions deploy each according to its individual Strategy Rating. Any ties are resolved by a D6 roll-off.

    Default Strategy Ratings†

    Faction Strategy Rating
    Space Marines 5
    Eldar 4
    Orks, Chaos 3
    Imperial Guard, Squats, Sisters of Battle 2
    Tyranids 1

    † Certain characters can alter a faction's Strategy Rating when selected to lead it.

  10. Decide Who Goes First

    To determine who goes first, players roll a D6 and add the result to the Strategy Rating of their army's main faction—the highest total goes first. Players may alternatively agree who goes first based on the narrative thread of the scenario.

  11. The Turn Sequence

    The game is split into turns, with each turn divided into five phases. Each player alternates taking their turn, progressing through all five phases of the Turn Sequence.

    The Turn Sequence is as follows: Movement, Shooting, Hand-to-Hand Combat, Psychic, Rally.

  12. Determine the Winner

    When the last turn is done, each side totals the Victory Points it has taken. The larger total wins.

    Alternatively, the winner is determined by the Win Condition of the scenario.

Models move up to their Movement rate in any direction. Not all models in a unit are required to move, provided Squad Coherency is maintained; for example, part of a squad may be repositioned while a model with a Move or Fire weapon is left stationary, allowing it to still shoot. Eligible models may also Go into Hiding.

A model may turn to face any direction at no cost, and turning does not count as moving. A model carrying a Move or Fire weapon may therefore turn and still shoot.

A Fortification follows the rules below in addition to whichever Buildings rules apply.

A Fortification is a prepared defensive structure—a bunker, tower, stronghold or wall section. Each has its own datafax giving its capacity, access, fire arcs, deployment and the Armour Value of every location, front and side/rear.

These rules govern the larger Fortifications. Trenches, razorwire, emplacements and concealed bunkers carry their own rules for access and damage on their own datafaxes, and are not covered here.

Access

Troops enter a Fortification only through the steel doors in its walls, and only where the model is physically small enough to pass. A dreadnought, Tyranid or Ogryn cannot enter unless the Fortification was purpose-built for it.

Take a model that enters off the table and place it on that Fortification's floor plan, one model to a square. Moving one square costs 1" of the model's Movement. Changing level means moving into a square beside a ladder, at the cost of the model's entire movement; it arrives beside the ladder on the new level, and may still fire or fight that turn.

Every level has a trapdoor and every Door a lock, so occupants may seal a Fortification against enemy models entering or changing level.

Firing Out

Each Vision Slit allows one model to fire from it, restricted to a 90° arc straight through it; where floor plans are in use it fires through the slit on the side of the square it occupies. Models on the roof shoot under the normal rules.

A Firing Port is a fixed sponson on a larger Fortification, taking two squares of the floor plan—one for the weapon, one for the gunner. Any model in the owning player's army may act as gunner, provided it stands on the gunner's square and has not moved that turn. A Firing Port fires within a 180° arc centred on itself. No more than one Vision Slit in three may be replaced with a Firing Port.

Support Weapons

The roof of a Fortification whose datafax allows it may carry a Support Weapon, counted as dismantled and reassembled there. Nothing moves it to the roof mid-battle, and one set up there stays for the duration. A Mole Mortar may not be set up on a roof. A Support Weapon may be set up inside a Fortification, but may not fire out of it.

Attacks on Fortifications

Models that shoot at a Fortification may either attack the models on its roof or the Fortification itself—models inside are beyond direct attack, no matter that they fired out the turn before. Models on the roof are attacked under the normal rules and receive the -2 hit modifier for being in Hard Cover.

A Fortification is a large stationary target. At Long Range it counts as a Large Target for +1 To Hit, and at Short Range it is hit automatically.

Roll for hit location and damage on the Fortification's datafax, as for a vehicle. Only a direct hit affects a Fortification. A weapon with a Blast Marker that strikes models on the roof, or that Scatters onto the Fortification or a nearby target, damages only the models on the roof; one that hits the Fortification directly damages a single location, chosen at random.

A Fortification may also be attacked in Hand-to-Hand Combat, exactly as a vehicle is.

Doors, Vision Slits & Firing Ports

A model within 6" of a Door with a clear Line of Sight to it may shoot the Door directly. The hit is automatic—roll neither to hit nor for location. A trapdoor may be attacked the same way by a model on the roof or in the same section; it has an Armour Value of 15 and uses the Door Damage table.

Once a Door is destroyed, later hits on that location pass through the doorway and strike a randomly chosen model inside.

A model inside 6" of a doorway or trapdoor that has been destroyed, or within 1" of a Vision Slit, may fire or lob a grenade through it at a model within, rolling to hit and to wound as usual.

Nothing may be fired or thrown through a Firing Port, which has no slit to shoot through. A Firing Port may still be hit by rolling for location, or attacked in Hand-to-Hand Combat.

Special Weapons

The weapons below reach the models inside a Fortification, or damage the structure in a way of their own. Where a datafax divides a larger structure into sections, each of them affects one section only.

A Harlequin's Kiss used within 1" of a Vision Slit may strike any model inside, resolved on the Vehicle Crew Penetration Chart.

A Hand Flamer, Flamer or Heavy Flamer hits a Vision Slit automatically and washes through it. Each model inside rolls a D6, and is caught on a 3 or more. Flamers take none of the bonuses a Blast Marker weapon has inside a Building.

A Graviton Gun that hits ignores Armour Penetration altogether, and adds 1 to its roll on the damage chart for the location it struck.

Where any part of a Fortification falls under a Distort Cannon template, roll a D6: on a 4 or more the structure and every occupant are caught, and a single test settles them all.

Gas from a Choke, Hallucinogen, Scare or Toxin Grenade seeps in through the Vision Slit. Where the marker covers the front of the structure, each model inside rolls a D6, and on a 3 or more may be affected as the grenade's own entry describes.

A Photon Flash Flare outside the structure does nothing to those within. One that goes off inside catches every model there, adding 1 to the roll on the Flash Effect Chart.

A Vibrocannon damages a Fortification as it would a vehicle. The hit is automatic, the structure has an Armour Value of 22, and a penetration is resolved on the Structure Damage Chart with 3 added to the roll.

A Mole Mortar attacking a Fortification uses the chart below in place of its own accuracy chart.

When a unit is required to make a Leadership Test, the player rolls 2D6 and compares the score against the unit's Leadership. If the score is less than or equal to it, the unit passes. If, however, the score is higher, the unit fails the test and suffers the effect of whatever triggered it.

If a model or unit has the Infiltration ability, it can be placed on the table after both armies have been deployed, instead of during the standard deployment sequence. Infiltrating units may be placed anywhere in the Battle Zone that is not in Line of Sight of any enemy model. If they are placed behind or within concealing terrain, they may start the game in Hiding. If both sides intend to deploy infiltrating units, they must each roll a D6—with the lowest score deploying first.

A linked weapon is a matched pair mounted to fire as one, sighted on the same spot and triggered together—the twin lascannon of a Land Raider, or the twin autocannon of an Ork warbike.

Firing a Linked Pair

A single roll To Hit settles the pair: on a hit both weapons strike, and on a miss neither does.

Resolving a Linked Hit

Both shots land together, and each is then worked out on its own. Against an ordinary model that means rolling twice to wound, and taking two armour saves where both wound. Against a vehicle it means rolling Armour Penetration and Damage once for each weapon—though the two land so close together that one roll fixes the location for both.

Linked Sustained Fire

Where the pair has Sustained Fire, roll to hit as though a single weapon were firing. A hit then rolls the Sustained Fire dice of both weapons at once, and a jam on either silences the pair, though whatever they scored before jamming still counts.

There are occasions when a model may be forced to move irrespective of a player's wishes—these are Compulsory Moves. Common examples are vehicles that go Out of Control or models that become Frenzied, but numerous rules trigger such moves. Compulsory Moves always occur before Normal Moves.

A model driven into contact with an enemy this way has not charged, and takes none of the bonuses a Charge carries. Its opponent has every option it would have against a declared charge.

Mission Cards describe one or more objectives to be accomplished during a game—and the Victory Points awarded for doing so.

Faction Restrictions

Orks never take The Assassins or Witch Hunt—such tactics never occur to them.

The Tyranid player does not draw from the deck, but randomly selects a mission from a list of six—by rolling a D6 or using the randomiser.

Only Engage and Destroy, The Assassins, Witch Hunt, Hold the Line, and Take and Hold may be taken against Tyranids—the remaining missions assume bases to raid, ammunition to steal, or bunkers to assault.

The full list is available here.

Buildings provide both protection and tactical advantages—often improving fields of fire and making troops much harder to kill.

Movement in Buildings

Models may enter a Building in their move phase by moving through an unlocked door, open doorway or window. Doorways offer no movement penalty but entering through a window counts as crossing a wall of equivalent height. If a Door is locked, it must be Destroyed before models can move through. No fixed number may use one opening; the models' own movement rates set the limit.

Once inside, models move at their normal rate only, and may not Run. A Charge may be declared only against an enemy model in sight when the turn begins. Climbing to an adjacent level by ramp, stairway, escalator or lift occupies the whole Movement Phase; where a ramp or stairway is long enough to hold models, they cross it under the normal movement rules instead.

Shooting From Buildings

Models inside a Building may shoot through windows, doors, firing-slits and any other opening. A model at an opening stands behind Hard Cover, and shots against it take the To Hit Modifier for it. The width of the opening decides how many models may fire through it.

A model at a window or door may Hide, exactly as one behind an obstacle does. While hidden it may not be seen or shot at.

Blast Markers in Buildings

Two rules govern grenades and Blast Weapons used inside a Building.

Scatter is rolled as normal, and the result is then checked against the firer's Line of Sight. A Blast Marker whose centre finishes out of sight is pulled straight back towards the firer until that centre comes into view. A missile cannot otherwise scatter through a solid wall into the room beyond. Shots and grenades sent into a Building from outside are treated the same way, and may therefore come back at the firer.

A blast in a space too small to hold the whole marker gains +1 Strength and a further -1 Save Modifier. In such a space Template Weapons and gas weapons add +1 to the D6 roll which decides whether partially covered models are hit. Models on the far side of a solid wall from the centre of the marker are untouched, unless a window or doorway carries the blast through to them.

Hand-to-Hand Combat Inside Buildings

Hand-to-Hand Combat indoors follows the usual rules. A charge is still declared, and its target must be in sight when the turn begins.

Models fighting their way in through a window or door count the -1 Weapon Skill modifier for attacking across an obstacle, in the first round only. Once inside, neither side counts it.

A squad broken inside a Building makes for the nearest exits, which may leave it split between several of them. The models regroup once they are outside.

A Building that can be seen by true Line of Sight can be fired on. Anything 4" square or larger is hit automatically; smaller structures are hit as ordinary targets. Buildings are given an Armour Value and as such use Armour Penetration rules when being attacked.

Within their Firing Arc, a model must also be able to draw Line of Sight on a target to shoot at it. Line of Sight is always drawn from a "model's eye view". Where Line of Sight is blocked the target counts as obscured, and no shot may be taken at it. Line of Sight is blocked in the following cases:

  1. The target is behind solid Terrain, such as hills, rock formations, walls, and buildings, which completely cover it. Line of Sight blocking terrain is usually agreed by both players during Terrain Setup.

  2. Targets are obscured if there is an area of woodland Terrain more than 2" deep between them and the shooter.

  3. An obstacle of about a model's own height—a wall, a hedge, a row of scrub—blocks Line of Sight, unless it only partly obscures what stands behind it, as sparse bushes or a chain-link fence do. A model showing above such an obstacle can shoot and be shot at, counting the obstacle as Cover.

  4. Any interposing models—friend or foe—block Line of Sight.

House Rule

Many players let the second rank of a unit draw Line of Sight through the first, with the exception of Template Weapons. This is not a printed rule.

Vantage Points

When a model is positioned on top of a building, hill, or other Vantage Point, it may be able to draw Line of Sight and shoot at models that would otherwise be obscured. It runs both ways: a model that can see a target can be seen and shot at by it in turn.

If the outnumbered model survives the first Combat Round, each model facing it gains +1 Attack Dice and +1 Combat Score in the second Combat Round, +2 and +2 in the third, and so on.

If a model has killed all of its Hand-to-Hand Combat opponents, it may immediately make a Follow-Up Move—regardless of whose turn it is. When making a Follow-Up Move, the model moves up to 2" in any direction. Crossing a wall or other obstacle costs it nothing, though Terrain penalties apply as they normally would. This move can be used to engage another model (or multiple models) in Hand-to-Hand Combat—but does not apply the Combat Score Modifier for charging. A combat joined this way is not fought in the phase it began: the models are left in contact and resolve it in the next Hand-to-Hand Combat Phase, engaged and unable to act until then. If the model does not end its Follow-Up Move engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat, it may Move and Shoot normally in its next turn.

Heroic characters are an army's leaders and heroes. Unless stated to the contrary, a character moves and fights as an individual, picking targets freely—the standard rules for Choosing A Target do not bind them unless they are firing a Heavy Weapon.

Leading Squads

A character may join any squad by moving to within 2"—Standard Squad Coherency—of it and declaring that they are leading it. The squad may then use the character's Leadership for any Leadership Test it takes—Psychology, Rally and Break tests alike.

A character who has joined a squad may leave it whenever they wish—except while the squad is affected by Psychology, has declared a Charge, or is engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat. A character may not join and leave the same squad in one turn, but may leave one squad and join another.

Where a squad declares a Charge, any character who has already joined it must charge with it and fight in the combat that follows. A character may always charge alone instead, leaving the squad behind.

A character leading a squad counts as part of it in all respects. Should the squad be Broken, the character is Broken with it, fleeing in the open or going to ground in cover as the squad does. A character Immune to Psychology is the exception, and Broken Troops gives the rule.

Psychology is tested for separately. Where a character is subject to a rule the squad is not, they test alone and react alone; this may draw them away from the squad.

Champion-level characters (excluding Psyker Champions) are always members of a squad and cannot leave it.

Targeting Characters

A character standing more than 2" from every other unit may be fired at only when it is the closest target. If a character is within 2"—Standard Squad Coherency—of models at least as large as it and it is not the leader, then it cannot be selected as a target for shooting, even by other characters. If the unit within Standard Squad Coherency of the character is hit, the hit(s) are randomised across squad members and character together.

A hit allocated to the character is rolled to wound, and saved, against the character's own profile.

The Psychic Phase is the only optional phase in the game—if no Psyker capable of using powers remains, and no Psychic Power is currently in play, the phase is skipped entirely. It is recommended to master Movement, Shooting, Hand-to-Hand Combat before incorporating psionics into gameplay.

Running allows models to double their normal Movement. All models in a squad must run together and if they do so they cannot fire their weapons during the Shooting Phase.

A squad with an enemy model within 8" may not run—it moves normally or Charges.

In the original rulebook, the following also applied to the rules for Running:

If running troops move to within 8" of enemy troops then they immediately halt and ready their weapons.

The purpose of Charging is to move models into Hand-to-Hand Combat—no model joins Hand-to-Hand Combat except by charging. A squad charges as one body, travelling as much as double its normal Movement. Each charging model must attempt to engage the nearest enemy model, but may choose to ignore models already in Hand-to-Hand Combat. If, because of Compulsory Moves, another enemy model is closer than the charging model's originally declared target, the charging model must target the nearer model instead.

A charge is considered successful if the charging model can achieve base-to-base contact with an enemy model. If the enemy model is behind cover—such as a wall—the charging model must reach base-to-base contact with that instead. If no enemy model can be reached, the charger moves its full charge distance, stops, and may do nothing else for the rest of the turn. Models may be charged even if they are in Hiding.

Once Warp Cards have been dealt, Psykers may begin using their powers. Play proceeds as follows:

  1. The player whose turn it is nominates one of their Psykers and uses one of that Psyker's powers. Psykers can only use their own powers—never those belonging to another Psyker.

  2. A power is used by choosing its Psychic Power Card and setting it down face up, with enough Force Cards from hand to activate it. No power comes free—one force card at least, and the potent ones ask more; the card itself states the number.

  3. Once a Psychic Power Card is played, the opposing player may attempt to cancel it with a Nullify Card.

  4. Unless successfully Nullified, work out the effects as described on the Psychic Power Card.

  5. The force cards spent on the power then go face up onto a discard pile on the tabletop. The used psychic power card is placed face down in front of the player—it cannot be used again until the next Psychic Phase. If a power's effects last for multiple turns, the card remains face up on the table to indicate it is still in play.

Play passes back and forth this way until neither player has powers left to use. If a player plays Energy Drain, the phase immediately ends.

During the Psychic Phase, if Special Warp Cards are drawn, they may be played or retained as per the card's individual rules.

A model may only select targets within a 90° arc to its front, unless stated otherwise on its datasheet—this is its Firing Arc. If it is unclear what the "front" of a particular model is, the player who owns it may declare a location, but this must then not change for the entire game. If a potential target is right on the edge of a model's Firing Arc, then it can be targeted on a D6 roll of 4+.

Each Psychic Power carries its rules on the card itself, and in most cases that is enough to resolve its effects without issue. However, confusing or apparently contradictory situations can arise—these guidelines resolve the most common ambiguities. If a situation arises where there is not a clear resolution, the players should discuss it and try to agree on a solution—if no agreement is reached, roll a D6 to decide who is right, then carry on playing.

Shooting-Type Psychic Attacks

Quite a few Psychic Powers operate like firing a weapon in the Shooting Phase. Normal Firing Arcs do not constrain them; they may be sent out in any direction the Psyker likes. Shooting-Type psychic attacks do not use the rules for Choosing a Target, even when used by squads—such as Grey Knights or Daemons.

There are two kinds of Shooting-Type attack:

Strikes the First Model in its Path

The attack runs out in a straight line and strikes the first model along it. The Psyker must have a clear Line of Sight to the intended target. Should some other model—friend or foe—turn out to stand in the attack's path, that model is struck in the intended target's place—players should be careful to check this before committing to their shot.

Draws a Straight Line

The attack affects every eligible target along a line up to the Psychic Power's maximum range. Unless specifically stated, neither terrain nor models block these powers, which damage everything they pass over.

A variant lets the psyker set a template against their own base and send it away in a chosen direction. These work as described above and follow the rules for Remains in Play.

Other Psychic Attacks

Some Psychic Powers let the Psyker set a template anywhere inside the stated range. No line of sight is needed, and neither models nor terrain in between can stop them. Placement is free—no model need be chosen as the template's centre—and everything beneath it is hit automatically unless the Psychic Power Card says otherwise.

Other psychic attacks work nothing like shooting: they are aimed at a model or squad anywhere within the card's range. Some Psychic Powers can only be directed at single models; others only at squads. If a Psychic Power specifies a single model as the target, it can be used against any chosen model within range, regardless of whether it is part of a squad. Psychic Powers which target squads can be used against any group of models moving together as a squad, support weapons including their crews, and character models or large creatures standing alone, outside any squad's coherency distance. Hits are apportioned randomly in the same way as Firing Into Hand-to-Hand Combat.

Range

Measure range base to base, Psyker to target. A power used on a squad takes effect if any one of the squad's models lies in range.

A template power may be set with the template's centre at the full stated range from the Psyker's base.

Some squads can use Psychic Powers. Their ranges are measured from the squad member nominated to use the power.

Armour Saving Throws apply against all psychic powers which inflict wounds, unless the power specifically states otherwise. Where a save is allowed, the attack's strength sets the modifier:

Characteristic Tests

Some Psychic Powers are resisted by rolling a D6 against a stated Characteristic. These function in a similar way to Leadership Tests—a successful roll is either less than or equal to the given Characteristic, as stated on the Psychic Power Card. A score of 6 always fails.

If a power affects a whole squad, make one roll for the squad using the trooper's Characteristic. A Heroic Character with the squad—champions included—rolls apart, against its own Characteristic.

Some Psychic Powers trigger Leadership Tests. As these affect the minds of their victims directly, re-rolls never apply, and no Leadership bonus applies for a Heroic Character inside Squad Coherency, nor for an army Commander within 12".

Break Tests

Some Psychic Powers cause Break tests—and one can force a further test on a squad that has tested once this turn already.

A squad broken out of Hand-to-Hand Combat during the Psychic Phase is attacked at once by its enemies as it disengages. This is resolved using the rules for Breaking Off.

Split Up Squads

Some Psychic Powers trap models and prevent them from moving; others move models around the battlefield. It is entirely possible for models to be split off from their squads as a result. For models bound by Squad Coherency, the following rules apply:

  • If a squad is divided by a Psychic Power, the two parts are treated as two separate squads until both parts are free of the power that split them—a part may be just a single model.
  • Once no longer affected by the Psychic Power, the smaller part must attempt to rejoin the larger part as soon as possible.
  • While trying to rejoin, the smaller part may not Declare Charges, attack enemies who are Breaking Off, or engage enemies in Hand-to-Hand Combat during Follow-Up Moves.
  • The larger part may continue to act as normal.
  • As soon as the two parts are within coherency distance, they act as a single squad again.

Remains in Play

Some Psychic Power Cards Remain in Play and continue to have an effect over multiple turns—to indicate this, they are placed face up in a suitable place on the table.

If a Psychic Power has ongoing effects, apply those effects at the start of each subsequent Psychic Phase—once Warp Cards have been dealt, and before any new power is played.

A card that Remains in Play cannot be used again while it does. It persists for the rest of the battle, or until: it is Nullified; the Psyker using it is slain (unless specifically stated); or the Psyker who cast it chooses to end it.

A Psyker may end a Remains in Play Psychic Power early. To do so, they must pick it up instead of playing a new Psychic Power. The card returns to their hand and cannot be reused until the following Psychic Phase.

Dealing Psychic Powers

Psychic Power Cards are dealt in two stages—first all Primary Discipline powers, then all Tertiary Discipline powers. Within each stage, cards are dealt one Psyker at a time, beginning at the highest Mastery Level and working down. At least one power must always come from the Primary Discipline before any Tertiary Discipline powers are drawn. If a player wishes to draw from a Tertiary Discipline, they must wait until all Primary Discipline draws have concluded.

Discarding & Redrawing

Once a Psyker has been dealt their cards, the player may choose to discard some or all in favour of randomly dealt replacements.

Only one round of redrawing is permitted per Psyker, per discipline. Any discarded cards are returned to the deck, shuffled in, and the replacement is drawn at random from the same discipline. The new cards must be kept.

By mutual agreement, players may redraw before returning discards to the deck.

Keeping Powers Secret

Once Psychic Power Cards have been dealt, players should keep them hidden until they wish to use them. Place the cards face down, keeping each Psyker's powers separate from one another. This is important because Psykers may not use each other's powers, even if they share the same disciplines.

When a squad becomes Broken, it is no longer able to participate in the standard Turn Sequence. If the squad is in cover, it will remain stationary and Hide when its next turn begins. If not in cover, the squad will flee 2D6" away from any enemy models and towards the nearest piece of cover. Whilst Broken, models will continue to move in this way until they can reach cover and Hide. Terrain penalties do not slow fleeing troops, though Impassable Terrain still bars them. Players may agree beforehand that fleeing troops entering some particularly treacherous ground, a marsh among them, are lost on a D6 roll of 1.

If a model which causes Fear or Terror moves within 8" of a Broken squad, it will immediately flee an additional 2D6".

When a squad Breaks during Hand-to-Hand Combat, or if it is Charged while Broken, it will attempt to Break Off from the combat and flee.

Heroic Characters

If a Heroic Character that is Immune to Psychology is attached to a squad which breaks, it is not Broken and may act normally. However, if its rules require it to remain with the unit, it must maintain Squad Coherency with the fleeing squad, though it may otherwise act freely.

Parrying

For every weapon a model has with the Parry rule, it can turn aside one attack during each Combat Round—however, this is always optional. Once both players have rolled their Attack Dice, the Parrying player may force their opponent to re-roll their highest scoring dice—the re-rolled result stands, even if it is better. Two opposing models that can both Parry cancel each other out, and neither forces a re-roll.

Hidden Models

A Hidden model cannot be seen and cannot be targeted during the Shooting Phase. If any model in a Hidden unit Moves or Shoots, the whole unit is no longer Hidden. Models can go into Overwatch while remaining Hidden, but they cease to be Hidden once they open fire.

Normally a Hidden model is revealed as soon as it moves; however, if a model begins its turn Hidden and moves only through concealing terrain, it will remain Hidden.

Hiding and going into Overwatch take a turn each: a model hides in one turn and goes into Overwatch in the next.

Going into Hiding

A model goes into hiding at the end of its Movement Phase if it either stood still or covered no more than its normal move—never after a Charge or a Run. Only a model standing in cover, or behind an obstacle that would conceal it, may hide at all. Cavalry cannot hide, nor can vehicles or models in Tactical Dreadnought Armour.

A squad hides whole or not at all. No part of one may hide while the rest of it stands in the open.

Spotting Hidden Models

Models can spot Hidden troops within a radius equal to their Initiative (in inches). A Hidden model is spotted as well where enemy models reach a position from which they can see around or over whatever conceals it.

A model that spots a Hidden enemy for itself makes it Detected, and that model alone may then fire at it normally.

Detecting Hidden Models

When even a single model in a Hidden unit is Detected, the entire squad ceases to be Hidden and becomes Detected. Some models also have equipment or traits that allow them to make Hidden enemies Detected from afar.

A Detected model is still out of sight to every model that has not spotted it, and those models may not target it directly during the Shooting Phase. Only a Blast or Template weapon may be fired at it. A model caught in such a weapon's area of effect is hit on a D6 roll of 4+, whether it is Detected or still Hidden.

Psychic activity ebbs and flows like a tide across the warp. The Warp Flux determines how influential Psychic Powers will be during a battle.

Determining the Warp Flux

The Warp Flux is written as so many D6—1D6, 2D6, 3D6 and upward. This number indicates how many Warp Cards are dealt in a given Psychic Phase.

The normal Warp Flux is 2D6. By mutual agreement, players may increase or decrease this value at the start of the game to increase or decrease the impact of the Psychic Phase.

Maximum Warp Flux

Regardless of the level chosen before the game, the Warp Flux may never exceed 1D6 for every psyker. Psykers which are killed, broken, or unable to use their powers no longer count towards this total.

A side left without Psykers still receives its Warp Cards as normal.

Nullify cards may be played against enemy psychic powers, although the attempt to cancel always requires a roll of 5 or 6. Force Cards—and the Energy Drain, Destroy Power, Psychic Duel, and Reflection cards—cannot be used.

A side without Psykers can therefore still attempt to cancel some enemy powers—representing the natural resilience of the victims and the chance of a power simply failing—but it is at a clear disadvantage in the Psychic Phase.

A vehicle cannot be engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat proper. A model may charge one in the Movement Phase and attack it in the Hand-to-Hand Combat Phase that follows, but the two are not locked in combat, and the movement of neither is restricted in their next turns.

Attacks on Vehicles

An attacking model hits automatically, once for each point of its Attacks characteristic. It chooses the location struck rather than rolling for it, provided that location is reasonably within reach. Resolve Armour Penetration and Damage as for a hit from shooting, adding the Bonus Penetration Dice for the attacker's Strength, or for the Strength of the weapon used where it has one. Against a vehicle that is immobilised or stationary, add a further 1D6.

Exposed Crew

Crew behind armour cannot be attacked in Hand-to-Hand Combat. Where a vehicle carries its crew outside or in an open-topped compartment, a model moving into contact must fight the crew rather than the vehicle, and models on foot always fight the nearest crew member. Resolve the combat as normal. Killing the driver sends the vehicle Out of Control in its next turn.

Ranged Weapons in Close Combat

By exception to the normal rules, an attacker may use a grenade or any ranged weapon that is not Move or Fire against a vehicle in close combat. Choose the location as with a close combat weapon and resolve damage the same way. Any area effect is ignored, and the weapon fires once only—Sustained Fire does not apply.

Robots & Dreadnoughts

A robot, dreadnought or any other machine with a Weapon Skill fights a proper Hand-to-Hand Combat under the normal rules. Attacks against it are resolved as for any other vehicle, but only close combat weapons, pistols and grenades may be used.

Skimmers

Troops on foot can bring a skimmer to close combat only where it has landed.

“It's Gonna Blow!”

Where a vehicle suffers a damage result that will make it explode, every model in base contact may put D6" between itself and the vehicle before the explosion is resolved. Like a Follow-Up Move this happens in the Hand-to-Hand Combat Phase whether or not it is that model's turn. A model moving away in this manner may not engage a new opponent.

A model shoots one weapon, or throws one grenade, in its own side's Shooting Phase, unless a weapon's own rules say otherwise.

Range is the distance from the shooter to its target, and a weapon's maximum range is the far end of its Long Range band. Measure once the target is nominated: a target lying beyond maximum range is missed outright, and any other shot counts as Short Range or Long Range as the distance falls.

To choose a target, the attacking player declares which unit is shooting and nominates its target. In general a model fires at the closest target, and every member of a squad fires at the same one; however, some exceptions apply:

  • Heroic Characters may be nominated to fire at any valid target; however, they are still bound by the rules for Targeting Other Characters
  • If a model within a unit is armed with either a Heavy or Special weapon, it may fire at a different target to the rest of its squad.
  • If a model within a unit cannot see the target nominated by other models in the unit, or has some other target nearer to it than its squad's is, it may select a different target.
  • A unit may be nominated to fire at targets from one of two groupings: Vehicles and Monstrous Creatures, or Human-sized Creatures and Smaller Creatures. The attacking player may choose which category to target, but must then select the closest eligible target within that group.
  • Smaller Creatures can be ignored as a target, unless they are within 6" of the unit being nominated to fire—in which case, they must be selected as the target.
  • A model in cover may be passed over for one in the open, even where the model in the open is the closest target.
  • Models engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat and models that are Broken may be ignored.
  • Buildings or specific game objectives may always be chosen as targets over any other targets. When a character model is also an objective—as specified in The Assassins or Witch Hunt—the rules for Targeting Characters may be ignored for those characters.

Choosing a Target with Unusual Weaponry

When firing a Blast or Template weapon, all rules for Choosing a Target apply. In addition, the template must be placed so that most models under it are within the target unit. Clipping another unit behind or beside the closest unit is acceptable; however, clipping the target unit to reach another unit is not permitted.

When firing a Sustained Fire weapon, first follow the rules for Choosing a Target, and then the Sustained Fire rules.

Splitting Fire

Because models in the same unit may select different targets based on what they can see, players may position models during the Movement Phase so that their Firing Arcs cover different areas, allowing the unit to split its fire.

Vehicles and support weapons are commonly organised into units on the battlefield—vehicles into Squadrons, support weapons into Batteries. A squadron or battery usually consists of units with similar capabilities; the specific types may vary, provided every member can maintain a similar speed.

Support Weapon Batteries

Any support weapon costing under 100 points must belong to a battery. An army with three or fewer support weapons must form a single battery. An army with up to six may form up to two batteries of approximately equal size; with up to nine, up to three batteries, and so on.

For example, a force containing three Thudd Guns and two Rapier Laser Destroyers could field batteries of three and two, or all five as one—but not two batteries of two and a lone weapon.

Support weapon batteries observe the following:

  1. A battery deploys at the start of the game as one group of models, the way a squad does. It may be set up in terrain ordinarily impassable to it—woods or buildings, say—its crew having cleared a position before the battle; a support weapon so placed cannot move for the rest of the game.

  2. Batteries are subject to the Squadron & Battery Coherency rules below.

  3. If a battery takes a special action—such as Overwatch or Hiding—every weapon in the battery must take the same action, just like an ordinary squad.

  4. Each weapon in a battery picks its own target, within the limits of Choosing a Target. Fire directed at a battery goes against whichever support weapon stands nearest the attacker.

  5. Batteries take Break Tests like squads: if 25% of a battery's support weapons are destroyed in one turn, the survivors must test. A support weapon counts as destroyed once the weapon is wrecked or the whole crew is dead. Batteries test with +2 added to their crew's Leadership, to a maximum of 10. Servitor-crewed support weapons never take Break Tests.

  6. If a battery fails its Break Test, crews in cover hide—the crew cannot be shot at unless spotted, though the support weapons remain legitimate targets. Crews in the open flee 2D6" towards the nearest cover like ordinary Broken Troops, abandoning their weapons until they Rally and return to them.

  7. Victory Points are scored for batteries as for squads—for a battery with 50% or more of its weapons destroyed, and again for a battery destroyed entirely or broken at the end of the game.

Vehicle Squadrons

An army containing three or fewer vehicles worth less than 100 points each must form them into a single squadron. An army with up to six such vehicles may form one squadron or two of approximately equal size; with up to nine, up to three squadrons, and so on.

For example, a force containing two Warbikes, two War Buggies, and a Wartrak could field a squadron of two vehicles and a squadron of three, or a single squadron of five—but not two squadrons of two and a lone vehicle.

Troop Transports & Bike Squads

Vehicles used for Transporting Troops are under no obligation to squadron, though the player may place them in one. A squad mounted on Bikes follows the squadron rules yet adds nothing to the army's vehicle total—each bike-mounted squad is, in effect, a separate squadron.

The following rules apply to vehicle squadrons:

  1. A squadron deploys at the start of the game as one group, squad-fashion, and never in terrain impassable to it.

  2. Squadrons are subject to the Squadron & Battery Coherency rules below.

  3. One speed serves the whole squadron: a single speed counter covers every vehicle in it, placed at the turn's start as described in Moving Vehicles. Likewise, if any vehicle in the squadron goes into Overwatch, the whole squadron must do so.

  4. Each vehicle in a squadron may give every weapon a separate target, within the limits of Choosing a Target. Fire directed at a squadron goes against whichever vehicle stands nearest the attacker.

  5. A vehicle squadron is Immune to Psychology and never takes Break Tests.

  6. Victory Points are scored for squadrons as for squads—for a squadron with 50% or more of its vehicles destroyed or disabled, and again for a squadron with every vehicle destroyed or disabled at the end of the game.

Squadrons of vehicles worth more than 100 points each—such as Land Raiders or Dreadnoughts—may also be fielded, although such vehicles are under no obligation to form squadrons. In this case, every vehicle in the squadron must be of the same type—a Land Raider squadroned with two Predators is not allowed.

Characters

A vehicle ridden by a Character adds nothing to the army's vehicle total when squadrons are formed. Likewise, a character mounted in or on a vehicle worth less than 100 points is not subject to the squadron rules, but may be placed in a squadron if the player wishes.

Squadron & Battery Coherency

Coherency binds the vehicles and support weapons of a squadron or battery, as Squad Coherency binds an ordinary squad. Squadron and battery coherency distance is 6"—no vehicle or support weapon may move more than 6" from the rest of its unit.

A model that ends up more than 6" from its squadron or battery because another model is destroyed suffers no morale penalty, unlike an infantry squad—the unit's communication net is superior, and its crews are more used to fighting individually.

Coherency may be broken temporarily while moving—to avoid a collision, for example. At the end of the game, however, any vehicle or support weapon more than 6" from its squadron or battery counts as destroyed when calculating Victory Points.

Support weapon crew must remain within 4" of their weapon at all times, unless they flee or the weapon is destroyed. The crew of a destroyed weapon may join another support weapon in the same battery. A crew member acting as a spotter for Mole Mortars is not subject to coherency—a single crew member may act as spotter for every Mole Mortar in a battery.

Dismounted crews from individual vehicles follow the normal rules for Crewing Vehicles and do not have to maintain squadron coherency.

Any crew member may fire one of the vehicle's weapons in the Shooting Phase, the driver included. A weapon fires only within the Firing Arc given on the vehicle's Datafax.

Linked Weapons

Weapons mounted to fire in tandem are Linked Weapons, and count as a single weapon: one crew member fires them with one action, and all of them fire at the same target.

Roll once to hit. On a hit every linked weapon hits; on a miss every one misses. Against a vehicle, roll once for location—all of them strike the same point—then roll Armour Penetration and damage separately for each weapon. Against any other target, roll to wound and take a saving throw separately for each weapon.

Where linked weapons have Sustained Fire, roll to hit as though a single weapon were firing, then roll the Sustained Fire Dice for all of them together. A Weapon Malfunction on any of those dice jams every linked weapon; resolve any hits before the jam takes effect.

Passengers

Troops the vehicle is Transporting may fire from it in their own Shooting Phase. In an open-topped vehicle every model aboard may fire, provided it does not fire over the head of another model; the driver's head is no obstruction.

In an enclosed vehicle the number that may fire depends on its doors and hatches. Count an access hatch or door as room for two models to fire through, and a firing slit or viewport as room for one.

Some combatants are beyond the reach of dread. Where a unit entry, wargear, or army list designates a model Immune to Psychology, it ignores Fear, Terror, and every other Psychology rule on this page. It cannot be affected by them, and cannot choose to be.

Some weapons fire a short-range jet—energy, burning chemicals, etc. These weapons do not roll To Hit; instead they use one of the three Flamer Templates, as indicated on their Weapon Profile. Template Weapons do not roll To Hit in the conventional manner; instead, the template is laid down with its point against the firing model's base and its rounded end over the chosen target. Any models entirely covered by the template are hit; any models partially covered by the template are hit on a D6 roll of 4+. Damage and Armour Saves are then resolved as normal.

Some troops can become Frenzied—be it ritualistic, drug-induced, or simply their nature. Frenzied models go into a berserk rage if there are enemies within charge range at the start of their turn; this continues until they are either Broken in Hand-to-Hand Combat or there are no more enemies in charge range. Whilst a model is Frenzied, the following rules apply:

  1. If there are enemy models within charge range, the model must engage them in Hand-to-Hand Combat—this happens as a Compulsory Move.

  2. The model doubles its Attacks characteristic.

  3. It may not Parry.

  4. Frenzied models always use their Follow-Up Move and must use it to move closer to the enemy and engage in Hand-to-Hand Combat if possible. They may not use a Follow-Up Move to enter cover.

  5. The model is not required to take any other Psychology tests.

A Frenzied unit is Restrained by a Leadership Test passed at the start of its turn. Restrained troops ignore the effects of Frenzy for that turn.

If a Frenzied unit is Broken in Hand-to-Hand Combat, they cease to be Frenzied. If they later Rally, they do not regain their former Frenzy.

A Heroic Character leading a Frenzied squad must accompany its charge, but does not become Frenzied unless subject to the rule in their own right.

Some warriors fight to the last without faltering. A model designated as Never Breaks—by its unit entry, wargear, or army list—never Breaks. Any Leadership Test demanded of it passes automatically, and nothing can Break it.

A model may attempt to disengage from Hand-to-Hand Combat and escape. During the combat the model attempting to break off fights with a Weapon Skill of 0, and may not Parry. If the escaping model survives, it moves 2D6" directly away from its attacker. The retreating model and its squad are automatically Broken and may not attempt to Rally until the following turn.

Robots, Dreadnoughts, Greater Daemons, and Chaos Champions riding Juggernauts may move out of Hand-to-Hand Combat in their Movement Phase—and may then Charge or Shoot as normal. However, if they are engaged with another model in this category, the standard Breaking Off rules apply.

In Warhammer 40,000 there are many different types of troops, from normal humans to gene enhanced Space Marines, and from haughty but human-like Eldar to the eldritch horror of the Tyranids. To represent this, nearly every model in the game has a set of numerical characteristics.

Movement (M)

The number of inches a model can move on the tabletop under normal circumstances.

Weapon Skill (WS)

A model's WS indicates how capable they are at Hand-to-Hand Combat—the higher the number, the more skilled the model is.

Ballistic Skill (BS)

A model's BS measures how skilled they are at Shooting—models with a higher score are better shots.

Strength (S)

Strength reflects a model's ability to do damage in Hand-to-Hand Combat. S indicates how easily a model can convert hits into damage and can contribute to Armour Penetration.

Toughness (T)

Toughness represents a model's capacity to resist injury. The higher the models T rating, the harder it will be to damage.

Wounds (W)

W shows how many points of damage a model can sustain before it is removed from the table as a casualty. Most models have only 1 wound; however, larger creatures or particularly powerful characters may have more.

Initiative (I)

Initiative indicates how alert and agile a model is. This characteristic is used in situations which test a model's vigilance or reaction speed.

Attacks (A)

The base number of Attack Dice a model may roll during Hand-to-Hand Combat. Most models have only 1 attack; however, especially skilled combatants may have more.

Leadership (L)

The Ld characteristic represents how courageous, steadfast and self-controlled a model is in the heat of battle. It is used when making Break and Psychology tests.

Zero-Level Characteristics

Some models are given a score of 0 for certain characteristics. A zero means the model is wholly without that ability, or that the characteristic has no bearing on it. A common example is 0 BS for creatures such as Genestealers, which are unable to use ranged weapons

Characteristic Profiles

Orks and Gretchin do not draw on the warp as other races do—they generate their own psychic energy. Each Ork and Gretchin creates a weak psychic field, and in the excitement of battle these fields merge into a communal surge of energy known as the Waaagh!

This field interferes with the powers of other races, making Orks and Gretchin difficult to affect with psychic attacks—and it can be focused by Weirdboyz into devastating psychic assaults.

Weirdboyz in Battle

Ork armies do not include Psykers—they have Weirdboyz instead. A Weirdboy focuses the Waaagh! itself and does not gather power from the Warp Flux; energy pours in from the excited Orks and Gretchin nearby.

Like other Psykers, a Weirdboy receives Psychic Power Cards when the game begins—one power per Mastery Level, drawn from the Ork Weirdboyz discipline.

The Dangers of Waaagh! Power

During the Psychic Phase the Ork player receives half as many Warp Cards as the Warp Flux rolled—energy raised by the Orks themselves rather than pulled from the warp.

Before any psychic powers are played, each Weirdboy must test to control the power of the Waaagh! The power absorbed is determined by the single highest source on the chart below—sources are never added together—plus the hand-to-hand combat modifier where it applies.

A Weirdboy more than 12" from any Ork or Gretchin—so long as no hand-to-hand fighting happened in the phase before—escapes the Waaagh! power entirely. Such a Weirdboy works no psychic power and takes no control test, though its Warp Cards remain good for Nullifying enemy attacks.

The Benefits of Waaagh! Power

To a Weirdboy, every Warp Card is as good as a Force Card. A power requiring three Force Cards could, for example, be played with two Force Cards and a Nullify card counted as the third. A Special Warp Card spent this way is discarded as an ordinary Force Card would be, staying spent for the rest of that Psychic Phase, cancelled power or not.

A Weirdboy who absorbs a Waaagh! power of 4 or more generates one extra Warp Card. The extra card is added to the Ork player's hand and may be used by any Weirdboy. The card arrives whether or not the Weirdboy kept control—though the 'Eadbangerz Chart may promptly take it back.

Orks generate their own psychic energy and are unlikely to draw the attention of daemons. Daemonic Attack played on a Weirdboy bites only on a D6 roll of 6—and even then the usual D6 escape from being dragged into the warp remains open.

The Nullify and Special Warp Cards that arrive with the Warp Flux stand for the natural resilience of Orks and Gretchin—their innate toughness, not the Weirdboy's conscious effort, is what turns psychic attack aside.

Weirdboy Warpheadz

Warpheadz are Weirdboyz whose minds have become saturated with Orky power through long survival—manic, overconfident, and drawn to the thick of the fighting. A Warphead uses all the normal rules for Weirdboyz, but has a Mastery Level of 4 rather than the usual Weirdboy Mastery Level of 2.

Minderz

Four Minderz escort every Warphead, keeping base contact at all times. The Minderz fight normally as well as restraining their charge.

If all four Minderz are killed, the Warphead makes a Run move towards the biggest group of Orks available, trying to get within 12" of the best source of Waaagh! power. In the Psychic Phase, a Warphead without Minderz always uses a psychic power picked at random, and other Weirdboyz may only use their powers after the Warphead has done so. If there are not enough Warp Cards to play the randomly chosen power, there is no further effect, and other Weirdboyz may use their powers freely.

Madboyz

Warpheadz exert a strange influence over Madboyz. A Madboy within 2" of a Warphead may take Leadership Tests using the Warphead's Leadership of 8, even though Madboyz cannot normally benefit from a character's higher Leadership.

Shots may be worked out one model at a time, or rolled together where several identically armed models fire on a group and every shooter needs the same roll To Hit.

The dice which hit are then gathered up and rolled again for damage, provided the targets share a Toughness, and Armour Saves are taken the same way.

Where the target squad stands partly in Cover, the shots are either split into batches and rolled on their own scores, or the To Hit Modifier is averaged across the whole squad:

  1. Where more of the squad stands in the open than in cover, the cover modifier is ignored altogether.

  2. Otherwise, where any of the squad stands in the open, the cover modifier is reduced by 1.

  3. Where the whole squad is in cover, some in Hard Cover and some in Soft Cover, the soft cover modifier is counted for all of them.

Casualties are taken from the models nearest the firer, whatever those models carry. A trooper with a special weapon is no likelier to fall than any other.

Where the nearest models cannot be told apart, a squad drawn up in a line being the usual case, casualties are randomised. Roll a D6 for each casualty inflicted, count that many models along the squad from the right, and remove the model reached. A model already removed is not counted twice while others remain.

A model may move in the Movement Phase and shoot in the same turn. Moving costs it nothing in accuracy.

A model which doubles its move may neither shoot nor throw a grenade that turn, whether by Charging or by Running. Cavalry which charge or gallop are bound by the same restriction.

A weapon carrying the Move or Fire rule may not be fired in a turn in which its bearer moved. Cavalry are restricted exactly as foot troops are.

A Passenger shooting from a vehicle is the exception, since the vehicle moves rather than the model.

Hate is a powerful emotion. In the galaxy of the 41st millennium, it is fuelled by endless rivalry and grudges borne over tens of centuries. When a model harbours Hate for an adversary, the following rules apply:

  1. Units take Break & Rally tests with a Leadership value of 10.

  2. When fighting in Hand-to-Hand Combat with a Hated foe, models may re-roll any attack dice in the first turn of combat.

  3. Models must always make a Follow-Up Move towards their Hated enemy and engage them in Hand-to-Hand Combat, if they are able to do so.

A Heroic Character leading a squad that Hates its enemy must follow up with it. The re-rolls and the Leadership value of 10 apply only to a character who Hates that enemy in their own right.

Opposing models are kept at least 1" apart, and no model may move closer than that to an enemy unless it is charging.

To engage an enemy unit in Hand-to-Hand Combat by charging it, the intention must be declared at the very start of the Movement Phase. To declare a charge, each model—or group of models—in the attacking unit nominates a target for its charge. Each charging model goes for the closest enemy model not already engaged, so a squad whose nearest opponents are taken by its leading models may find the rest charging a different enemy unit altogether†.

The attacking player must be reasonably confident that the charging unit can reach its target; however, the distance may not be measured before declaring the charge. Charging troops must have a clear run at their target—they cannot charge through other models, and any terrain features should be taken into account.

Once a unit has been declared as charging, it may not participate in the Shooting Phase, even if it fails the charge.

† The rulebook declares a charge squad against squad; its reference sheet has a squad charge the nearest enemy. A White Dwarf Q&A settles the two: a charging model goes for the closest unengaged model.

Certain ranged weapons fire projectiles capable of attacking models within a certain radius; these are known as Blast Weapons. To shoot a Blast Weapon, select a target as normal and roll To Hit. If the nominated target is not in range, then the shot automatically misses and has no effect. If the shot hits, then position the correct Blast Marker centred over the target model—this model is hit. Additionally, any other models whose entire bases are covered by the marker are hit. Any models whose bases are partially covered by the marker are hit on a D6 roll of 4+. No To Hit Modifier applies to that roll—neither cover, nor target speed, nor anything else.

Scattering

When a Blast Weapon misses, a Scatter roll is made. Roll a Scatter Dice and an Artillery Dice together, then consult the following chart:
