Maximum Scatter

A shot can never scatter more than half the distance between the shooter and the nominated target. If the Scatter Roll exceeds this limit, reduce the scatter distance accordingly. A scattered shot may come to rest outside the firer's Firing Arc.

Throwing Grenades

A model carrying grenades may throw one in place of shooting. Roll To Hit on the thrower's Ballistic Skill, then wound and save as for any other shot. A grenade may be thrown 2" plus twice the thrower's Strength, to a maximum of 12".

If a grenade throw misses, then roll to Scatter, halving the result rolled on the Artillery Dice. The rules for Maximum Scatter do not apply when throwing grenades.

Targeting the Ground

Blast Weapons may also target the ground, instead of a model; this is particularly useful when using non-lethal ammunition such as Blind Grenades. When doing so, the standard To Hit roll—and any modifiers—are ignored. Instead, position the correct Blast Marker centred over a target location. The point must be visible to the firer and within the weapon's maximum range. On a D6 roll of 6 the shot successfully hits, but on a roll of 1-5 a roll to Scatter is then made, with one exception: a Hit & Misfire result is treated as an ↑ & Misfire instead.

Where the firer's own modified score would have been 7 or worse, the shot uses the 7+ To Hit procedure in place of the flat 6.

For every 1,000 points an army consists of—or part thereof—1 Strategy Card may be drawn at random. An army of 1,500 points therefore draws 2 cards.

Some special characters and items of wargear alter how many Strategy Cards a force draws, or negate particular cards. Any such exception is given in the relevant army list entry.

The Tyranids faction never draws Strategy Cards. Instead, they have special rules that are implemented directly before Strategy Cards are drawn.

Players fighting against Tyranids remove Virus Outbreak, Malfunction, and Traitor from the deck before drawing. Facing Tyranids, Crack Shot halves the target's Toughness, rounding up.

House Rule

Virus Outbreak is widely considered game-breaking, and most players remove it from the deck in all games. This is not a printed rule, but it has become standard practice, and the card is excluded by default when drawing at random here.

The full list is available here.

During the Rally Phase, eligible units which are Broken may attempt to Rally. To do so, they must pass a Leadership Test; if they pass then they may act normally from their next turn, otherwise they remain Broken.

Units are eligible to Rally if:

  1. They are in or behind Cover.

  2. They were not forced to flee this turn, for any reason.

  3. The nearest friendly unit is not also Broken.

If a unit is at 25% or less of its starting strength and is Broken, it may never Rally. The unit is considered destroyed, and any remaining models are immediately removed.

Insane Bravery and Craven Cowardice

When attempting to rally a Broken unit, if the Leadership Test scores a 2, the squad is truly roused and leaps straight back into the fight—they may immediately take a normal Turn, moving, firing, going on Overwatch or charging, though they do not fight Hand-to-Hand Combat in it. From the player's next turn the squad acts normally, and may be Broken again. If, on the other hand, the score is 12, then the squad's morale is irreparably broken—the unit is considered destroyed, and all models are immediately removed.

In the Hand-to-Hand Combat Phase, all models with a Weapon Skill value that are in base-to-base contact with an enemy model fight in Hand-to-Hand Combat—combat is mandatory for every eligible model, unless explicitly prevented by another rule. Both sides fight and can inflict casualties, regardless of which player's turn it is. Models can fight in a 360° arc, and there is no advantage to attacking a model from behind.

A model in base-to-base contact with an enemy is engaged, and until the combat is resolved it neither Moves in its Movement Phase nor Shoots in its Shooting Phase. Only Breaking Off releases it.

Some ranged weapons can fire a lengthy burst of projectiles; this is referred to as Sustained Fire. If a Sustained Fire weapon successfully hits its target, the firing player chooses at least one Sustained Fire Dice and up to the maximum indicated by Sustained fire X on the weapon's profile. The combined total of this dice roll determines the actual number of hits scored by the weapon. The first hit is always allocated to the original target; any additional hits may be assigned to other visible models within 4" of the location of the first hit. Damage is then resolved for each hit as normal.

Weapon Malfunctions

Each Sustained Fire Dice has a Jam result on one face. This result indicates the weapon has malfunctioned in some way—and the roll has failed to hit. A Jam on one dice does not stop other dice from scoring hits; however, multiple Jam results can occur simultaneously. A weapon may not be fired while it has one or more malfunctions caused by Jams—although if a model has other weapons, it may still use those. Instead of shooting at all, a model may spend its Shooting Phase clearing a single Jam—once the weapon has no more Jams, it can be used again.

A Jam cannot be cleared at all by a model on Overwatch, by one that is Broken, or by one engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat. A model that is running or hidden may still clear one. A hit from a Shotgun firing a Solid shell clears one Jam on the model it strikes†.

† A White Dwarf Q&A ruling; the rulebook gives no such effect.

House Rule

The rulebook does not say how a Jam works on a vehicle carrying several weapons. Most players apply the rules above to the gun and its gunner rather than to the whole vehicle, so one jammed weapon does not silence the rest. This is not a printed rule.

Each weapon profile has a Short and Long range To Hit value. This represents how well a given weapon performs at different ranges. A value of 0 conveys no benefit or penalty, a positive number improves To Hit, and a negative number impedes To Hit.

These values belong to Shooting alone. Pistols are carried into Hand-to-Hand Combat more often than any other weapon, and their To Hit values count for nothing there.

Wargear Cards represent the rare and specialised equipment carried by an army's leaders—bionics, relics, force fields and master-crafted weapons. Only Heroic Characters may be given them; ordinary troopers never carry one.

A character carries no more cards than their rank allows. The chart below gives that allowance, and applies equally to Ork bosses, Eldar Exarchs and their like. It stands unless the character's own army list entry supersedes it.

Card Allowance Chart

Champion, Psyker, Psyker Champion
1
Hero, Master Psyker
2
Mighty Hero, Psyker Lord
3

Each card's points value is printed on the card itself, and is added to the points value of the character carrying it. Chosen cards are written on the army roster.

Every card belongs to one of three rarity classes. The class is a rule rather than a label—it governs how many of that card an army may field.

Rarity Chart

Uncommon
Any number may be used, even where there are not enough cards for them. Uncommon items are restricted to characters, but not in limited quantities.
Rare
Limited to the number of cards published—further sets do not increase the number available.
Unique
An army holds at most a single copy of any Unique item.

Two of these limits are given as recommendations rather than rules. White Dwarf 195 recommends that Unique items are used only by the special characters listed as carrying them in an army list, and that another character may take one only if the opponent agrees before the battle starts. The Uncommon allowance is a recommendation on the same footing.

Restrictions

Rarity governs quantity alone. The restrictions printed on a card—a race, a troop type, or a named bearer—apply in addition, and are never set aside by it.

Some items are expended in use. Where a card says so, it is discarded once its effect has been resolved and may not be taken again for the rest of the battle.

Wargear in Play

A card stays with the character it was allocated to. If that character is killed their wargear is destroyed with them, and may not be salvaged by anyone else. Characters may not pass wargear from one to another during a battle.

A scenario whose objective is the capture of a device or piece of equipment may set this aside, but that is an exception rather than the ordinary case.

Two departures from the sources are worth noting. Codex Ultramarines states that a Wargear card cannot be allocated more than once, which applies the Unique restriction to every card; White Dwarf 195 is later and more precise, and the site follows it. The rulebook gives the allowance as a chart by rank while the codex gives it as the character's army list entry; neither says which governs, and the site treats the chart as the standing allowance and an army list entry as superseding it.

Every vehicle's Datafax gives its Motive Type, which governs the terrain it may cross:

  1. Tracked

    Unhindered over most terrain, and through woods at up to half Slow speed. Crosses Obstacles at Slow speed without penalty, and crashes if it attempts them faster. Crosses streams and fords freely, but may not enter deep water. On entering a bog or swamp at Combat or Fast speed, roll a D6; a 6 leaves the vehicle stuck fast for the rest of the game.

  2. Wheeled

    Obstacles of every kind are barred to it, as are woods. May not cross Difficult Terrain or Very Difficult Terrain at Combat or Fast speed.

  3. Bikes & Trikes

    May not cross Obstacles of any kind—a bike that attempts to crashes. Crosses Difficult Terrain and Very Difficult Terrain, including woods, at Slow speed only, and crashes at higher speeds. No water can be crossed beyond shallow streams and fords.

  4. Walkers

    Unhindered over any terrain except deep water; a river or sea bed can be walked at half rate. A wall above the model's knee stops it, though hedges and other light vegetation give way. May enter a Building through any opening the model physically fits through.

  5. Skimmers

    Crosses terrain features and Obstacles without penalty, and may end its move on top of one—though by agreement not where the model will not balance, such as a building or wood.

Psychic Powers only affect vehicles if the power card specifies a Strength value or includes explicit vehicle interaction rules—no other psychic powers can affect vehicles. This distinction prevents unintended game-breaking scenarios like Teleporting Land Raiders.

Targeting Vehicles

Vehicles—including any passengers and crew—are valid targets for psychic powers that specify squad as their target type, treated the same as any other squad-sized unit. For powers specifying a single model as the target, the target may not be an entire vehicle but may be a single hit location such as a track, weapon, or a single crew or passenger model.

Vehicle Hit Locations

How vehicle hit locations are determined depends on the attack type:

Strikes the First Model in its Path

Roll to determine which location is hit, exactly as if shooting at the vehicle with a weapon.

Draws a Straight Line

A vehicle in the path of such an attack takes an automatic hit on the first location contacted. Any other locations crossed by the line are hit on a D6 roll of 4+.

Template Attacks

Each vehicle location covered or partially covered by the template is hit on a D6 roll of 4+.

Armour Penetration

Each hit inflicted on a vehicle requires a separate armour penetration roll.

Some Psychic Powers state an armour penetration value directly on the card, and some bypass armour altogether to affect a randomly selected crew member. However, unless specified otherwise, psychic attacks with a Strength value must penetrate the vehicle's armour or hit an exposed crew member to deal damage.

A Psychic Power that does not specify an armour penetration value uses the standard Armour Penetration rules, adding the Bonus Penetration Dice for its Strength.

Certain weapons use volatile, burning-chemical ammunition. If a model survives a hit from such a weapon, it must roll a D6; on a result of 4+, they Catch on fire. At the start of its own turn a model that is on fire must make a Fire Test:

Fire Test Chart (D6)

1-5
The fire burns on, and another automatic hit lands—its damage worked out as one more automatic hit from the weapon that set the model alight. A survivor moves its full Move characteristic in a random direction given by a Scatter Dice; Squad coherency does not bind the model while it burns.
6
The flames are extinguished; the model is no longer on fire. It may not move or shoot for the rest of the turn, but it can act normally starting from its next turn.

While On Fire

During the Movement Phase, any friendly model that is eligible to do so may move within 1" of a burning model and attempt to beat out the flames. On a D6 roll of 6 the flames are put out. For each additional friendly model that helps +1 modifier is applied. Models that help a burning model may not shoot during the Shooting Phase.

Vehicles (Dreadnoughts included), models in Terminator Armour, Frenzied troops and Tyranids may simply disregard the flames and fight on unhindered.

Not all ground is equally easy to cross. To represent this on the tabletop, there are four types of terrain, each with an associated movement penalty:

  1. Open Terrain

    No penalty—woods, scrub, brush, boulders, crevasses, debris, ruins, stairs, ramps, steps.

  2. Difficult Terrain

    Cross at half Movement—thick forests, soft sand, marshes, streams, shallow water, steep slopes, ladders.

  3. Very Difficult Terrain

    Cross at quarter Movement—swamps, tar pits, pools, fast flowing rivers, almost sheer slopes.

  4. Impassable Terrain

    Cannot be crossed—sheer cliffs, very high walls, deep rivers, lakes.

Hills count as Open Terrain unless both players agree before the game to treat them as Difficult Terrain. The type of any other feature may be settled the same way.

A teleporter is a device built into a spaceship or a building, and it sets a squad on the battlefield directly. Squads allowed to teleport into a battle are named in their own army list.

A squad teleports in the Movement Phase. Place one model of the squad where the squad means to arrive, then roll the Scatter Dice and 2D10 to find where it lands.

A double 1 on the two D10 destroys the whole squad in a teleporter accident. Otherwise the model moves the distance rolled, in the direction the Scatter Dice gives. A hit deviates by the small arrow on that face, so an arriving squad always moves.

A model carried off the table edge has failed to arrive, and the squad may try again in its next turn. A model that comes down in a building, a vehicle or any other solid object deviates again from where it stands.

Once the first model is placed the rest of the squad goes anywhere within 2" of it. Teleported models may shoot and fight in Hand-to-Hand Combat in the turn they arrive, though arriving straight into a combat does not count as Charging.

A squad that has paid the points to teleport in may teleport out again. It is removed from the table in its own Movement Phase and does not return later in the game.

Teleport Homer

A teleport homer puts out a coded signal for a teleporter to lock onto. Where a squad teleports to a spot lying within 6" of a working homer—one carried by another squad, for example—a hit on the Scatter Dice locks the arrival on and it does not move at all. An arrow deviates it as usual.

If a unit has not Charged or made a Compulsory Move, it may forgo its turn and instead prepare Overwatch—a model preparing Overwatch may not move at all, not even to turn on the spot. Overwatch is declared at the start of the player's own turn. All models in a unit must enter Overwatch together. A unit on Overwatch does nothing for the rest of its turn, but may shoot at any time during the opponent's turn†—this lasts until the beginning of the unit's next turn.

A unit fires once from Overwatch: as soon as it shoots, its Overwatch is spent. Grenades may not be thrown as Overwatch fire.

A unit shot at while on Overwatch, whether or not the shot hits, takes an immediate Leadership Test. Failing it, the unit loses Overwatch and returns to the ordinary sequence.

† In the original rulebook, Overwatch shots were only permitted during the opponent's Movement Phase; this was later revised in a White Dwarf Q&A.

A skimmer hovers above the ground on gravitic motors. Its motive type is Skimmers, which governs the terrain it crosses.

Movement

A skimmer may land only at Slow speed and will crash if it attempts to land any faster. A skimmer that lands moves no further that turn, and may take off in a later Movement Phase at Slow speed. It may instead halt without landing, which is called hovering, and a hovering skimmer may turn by any amount. Troops may mount or dismount only while it is landed or hovering.

Out of Control

A skimmer goes Out of Control as any other vehicle, moving 3D6" in a random direction. Roll a D6 as well for its altitude.

Altitude Chart (D6)

1
The skimmer swoops down and crashes into the ground.
2-5
The skimmer stays at the same altitude.
6
The skimmer climbs sharply, stalls, and crashes to the ground 2D6" away, the direction given by the Scatter Dice.

Pop-Up Attacks

A skimmer that was stationary or moved at Slow speed in its previous turn may make a pop-up attack. Declare it in the Movement Phase; the skimmer moves upward instead of across the table. Models on Overwatch may shoot at it as it rises, and are usually the only models able to shoot at it at all.

In the Shooting Phase a popped-up skimmer traces Line of Sight as though up to 12" above the table, as may enemy models firing back on Overwatch. Add 12" to the range of any shot made at it; the skimmer's own shots take no such penalty. It drops back down once the attack is resolved, and in its next turn may pop up again or move off at Slow speed.

Overruns

A skimmer may not deliberately overrun troops on foot. The exception is a jet bike crew armed with close combat weapons, which may make Hit & Run Attacks as the rider of a bike does.

The Warp Deck has 36 cards in total, composed of: 22 Force Cards, 8 Nullify cards, and one each of Daemonic Attack, Destroy Power, Psychic Duel, Reflection, Ultimate Force, and Energy Drain.

Dealing Warp Cards

As each Psychic Phase opens, the Warp Flux is found by rolling the dice agreed before the battle and totalling them. That many Warp Cards are dealt, beginning with the player whose turn it is.

The Warp Deck is only reshuffled if the cards run out altogether and the deck must be started over again.

A vehicle can be driven out of control by damage, by a psychic attack or by an exotic weapon. Only a vehicle that moved in its previous turn can be affected; a stationary vehicle never goes out of control.

Move it as a Compulsory Move, before all other models. Roll a D6 for direction, then move the vehicle 3D6", capped at its maximum speed.

Out of Control Chart (D6)

1-2
The vehicle turns 45° to the left.
3-4
The vehicle continues straight ahead.
5+
The vehicle turns 45° to the right.

Some damage results send a vehicle out of control for one turn, after which it halts; others leave it out of control for the rest of the game, or until a collision stops it. Where the driver has been slain, another crew member may restore control, as given on the Datafax.

Some units cause Fear, and some units are afraid of certain weapons. A squad or Heroic Character model must take a Leadership Test in the following situations:

  1. The unit is charged by an enemy that causes Fear. If they pass, they may fight as normal. If they fail and are outnumbered by that enemy, then they are immediately Broken. If they fail but are not outnumbered, they fight at half Weapon Skill, rounding up, in the first round of Hand-to-Hand Combat, and may not fire at the charging enemy if on Overwatch. The test is taken once the charge has been declared and the enemy found to be within its charge distance.

  2. The unit wants to charge an enemy that causes Fear. If they fail, they may not charge and remain stationary for that turn. They may, however, still participate in the Shooting Phase.

  3. The unit is Hit by a weapon that causes Fear. This calls for an immediate Break Test rather than a test against Fear, whatever casualties the hit caused.

A squad outnumbered in Hand-to-Hand Combat by an enemy it fears takes a Break Test at the end of every Hand-to-Hand Combat Phase, whether or not it lost a quarter of its strength. A squad that is not outnumbered suffers nothing beyond the ordinary rules.

Models that cause Fear are not affected by enemy models that cause Fear. When they face enemy models that cause Terror, they only have to test for Fear.

Every vehicle has a Datafax—a single card recording its armament, movement and defensive capabilities.

The front gives the vehicle's weapons and their fields of fire, its speed at each movement rate, its Motive Type, its Ram Value, the number of crew it carries, its transport capacity and its points cost.

The back gives a hit location table and the Armour Value of each location, followed by the Damage tables for the hull and for each weapon.

Move vehicles during the Movement Phase, in any order relative to other units.

A vehicle has three move rates—Slow, Combat and Fast—each given on its Datafax as the greatest distance it may cover at that rate. Vehicles begin the game halted or at Slow speed, and may change speed by only one band per turn.

Turning

A vehicle travels directly forwards unless it turns.

Turning Chart

Slow
Any number of turns, each of up to 360°.
Combat
Up to two turns, each of up to 45°; both may be combined into a single 90° turn.
Fast
One turn of up to 45°, at any point in the move.

Measuring Turns

Place the turn template in front of the vehicle with its direction arrow aligned to the vehicle's facing, then turn up to 45° to the left or right. A turn may instead be estimated by eye if the opposing player agrees.

Arid terrain is an optional set of rules for battles fought in desert country, standing beside the ordinary Terrain rules rather than replacing them. Woods, jungle, rivers and streams do not occur in an arid region; hills and buildings do, and behave as they do anywhere.

Arid Features

Open ground is open terrain, save that nothing may be dug into it: no trench, no emplacement and no concealed bunker.

Rough ground is desert littered with scrub and loose rock. It costs nothing to move through, counting as open terrain, and troops may Hide in it.

A wadi is a steep-sided gully. It is Difficult Terrain to cross and open terrain to move along. Troops in a wadi may hide from anything outside it and count Hard Cover against fire from outside, but neither hide from nor gain cover against anything inside it. A unit hidden in a wadi may follow it along and stay hidden as it goes.

An oasis counts as a small wood. A model within 1" of its edge may fire out and be fired at with Soft Cover; deeper than that it can neither see out nor be seen. An oasis is Difficult Terrain to move through.

A rocky outcrop is Very Difficult Terrain and gives Hard Cover to troops behind it.

Dunes are Very Difficult Terrain to a wheeled vehicle and Difficult Terrain to everything else. Troops may hide in or behind them. Nothing may be dug into a dune and no building stands in one.

A sangar is a low wall of piled rock, raised where the ground cannot be dug. Troops behind one count Hard Cover against fire crossing its front, and no cover at all against fire from behind it. A sangar costs 10 points for each 2" of wall, has an Armour Value of 15, and is destroyed and removed by a single penetrating shot.

Arid Conditions

Wind-blown dust and the haze off the ground shorten sight in arid country. Every shot takes -1 To Hit at Short Range and -2 at Long Range.

A wheeled, tracked, hover or skimmer vehicle that moves throws up a cloud of dust; a walker throws one up only where it runs or charges. The cloud is as wide as the vehicle, runs from where it finished back to where it began, stands 12" high, and hangs there until the start of that player's next turn.

Nothing sees through a dust cloud, so no weapon needing Line of Sight fires through one. A unit within 1" of the edge of a cloud may fire out of it at -1 To Hit, and a unit outside may fire into it at a target within 1" of the edge on the same penalty.

In Warhammer 40,000, cavalry means any unit whose mount has a single wound. A mount with more than one carries special rules of its own instead. Rider and mount count as one model, and the mount leaves play with the rider when the rider dies.

A cavalry model takes its Leadership, Toughness and Wounds from the rider, and its Move from the mount; the mount's own Toughness, Wounds and Leadership are never used. Being mounted improves the armour saving throw by +1, and in Hand-to-Hand Combat the mount's Attacks characteristic joins the rider's own.

The points value of a vehicle includes its crew, except where the vehicle is bought as an upgrade for a character model, as bikes are. The number of crew required is recorded on the vehicle's Datafax; their characteristics and equipment are given in the army lists.

Boarding & Leaving

Boarding and dismounting work for crew as for any other model; however, if the driver leaves a vehicle while it is moving, the vehicle will go Out of Control in the next turn. A crew member who dismounts cannot operate the equipment they were using until they reboard. Dismounted crew stay within 6" of their vehicle; only its destruction releases them, whereupon the survivors band together as a unit of their own, bound by the normal Squad Coherency rules.

Psychology

While crewing a vehicle, a model is immune to Psychology and exempt from Break tests. A crew member who dismounts becomes subject to both as normal.

Taking Over a Crew Position

Any crew member can perform any role aboard the vehicle, and if a crew member is killed or injured, another can move to that position to take over. It takes an entire turn for a model to change positions, during which time it cannot perform any other actions. Adeptus Mechanicus Engineers, Techmarines, Squat Engineer Guildmasters and Ork Mekaniaks may likewise board a vehicle and take a position over. No other model may do so.

Some vehicles carry troops in addition to their crew. The number carried is given on the vehicle's Datafax as its transport capacity, counted in human-sized or smaller models. Ogryns, Space Marines in Terminator Armour and other models of equivalent size each count as two.

Any number of models may board or leave in a turn, up to the vehicle's capacity. Models leaving may do so at any point in the vehicle's move, interrupting it if necessary, and are placed touching its sides or rear; they may then make a normal move immediately. Squad Coherency must be maintained between those leaving and any remaining aboard.

Models may board a vehicle which spent the previous turn halted, or moving no faster than Slow, provided they end a normal move within 2" of its side or rear. The vehicle may then move off.

Troops may board or leave without risk while the vehicle is moving up to 10". Beyond that, each model sustains an automatic hit with the Strength and Save Modifier shown below, and suffers 1 wound if the save is failed.

Four structures follow the Fortifications rules and add something of their own. Smaller works—trenches, emplacements, concealed bunkers and razorwire—are covered under Field Defences instead.

Battle Towers

A battle tower is a bunker raised clear of the ground, floor and roof alike. The only way into it is through the door at its foot, up the stair and through the trapdoor above, and an assault must therefore destroy the door and then the trapdoor. Both follow the ordinary rules for a Door.

Its Vision Slits sit too high to reach from the ground. A model at the wall may neither lob a grenade through one nor charge a model firing from it, and the restriction runs both ways: a model within 2" of the tower wall cannot be shot at from a Vision Slit either. A battle tower may carry Firing Ports.

A battle tower may mount a turret, carrying any Support Weapon the army may take. The weapon follows its usual rules with a 360° fire arc, and falls with the tower when the tower is destroyed. No troops stand on the roof of a tower that carries one.

An Ork Traktor Kannon in a turret drags what it catches into the structure, which collides with it. Where its polarity reverses, the turret itself is torn off and dragged towards the target, and the weapon counts as destroyed.

An Imperial Guard force may buy a command relay in place of a turret, and only one structure in the force may carry one. A tower so equipped counts as a command section of Leadership 9. A command relay is hit and destroyed exactly as a turret is, and its cost sits with the army list.

Wall Sections

A wall section, or rampart, is a thin bunker meant to be joined end to end into a curtain wall, and joined to battle towers to close a fortress. It may not carry Firing Ports.

Each section has a door at either end, following the ordinary rules. It has no trapdoor, so its roof is reached only from an open-ended section or through a door in a battle tower or other structure.

Where two sections meet, their facing doors count as a single door rather than two. Destroying a rampart therefore opens both ends at once.

Strongholds

A stronghold is two battle bunkers and a battle tower built as one, and each part is destroyed separately and treated as a structure in its own right. Nothing else may be joined to a stronghold.

A stronghold is shot at under the ordinary rules, with one addition: a firer may aim high or low, declared before rolling for location. Aiming high adds 6 to the roll on the location chart, and aiming low rolls a D6 as usual.

Autofire weapons are built throughout a stronghold. They always count as being on Overwatch and fire only in the opposing player's turn, hitting on a D6 roll of 4 or more and doing damage as usual. Eldar structures mount Shuriken Catapults and every other kind mounts Boltguns.

The system tracks one target at a time, so at most five weapons bear on it, and their range is 12" whatever the weapon itself would reach. They fire at the closest target at the end of the opposing Movement Phase, or at a unit charging the stronghold; where more than one unit charges, the owning player chooses between them.

A stronghold's tower takes a turret as a battle tower does, and that turret may mount an anti-skimmer weapon instead. Anti-skimmer weapons count as being on Overwatch, fire only in the opposing player's turn, reach 24", and may fire at nothing but a Skimmer.

A turret may mount twin-linked heavy bolters; two hunter-killer missiles, which are Imperium only and carry no maximum range at all; twin-linked shuriken cannons or a scatter laser, both Eldar only; or four linked kustom kombi weapons, Orks only. Kustom kombi weapons are each resolved separately, and the 24" limit still applies. What each costs sits with the army list.

Interior doors join the sections of a stronghold. They follow the ordinary rules at an Armour Value of 15, save that a 6 on the Door Damage Chart counts as a 5, so destroying an interior door never damages the structure.

A stronghold may carry a teleport jammer at 50 points, which denies the opposing player both teleporting troops and warp weapons. A unit teleporting inside, or a Vortex Grenade or Distort Cannon striking the structure, is scattered: roll the Scatter Dice and 2D6, and a hit resolves as normal while an arrow throws the unit or the blast 2D6" the way it points.

Wraith Towers

A wraith tower is an Eldar portal to the webway and a source of psychic power. One may be taken by an Eldar player, or set on the table in any game an Eldar force joins, and never more than one. It is bought from the fortification allowance.

A Warlock, Farseer or Shadowseer within 6" of the tower may draw one extra Warp Card. No more than one extra card is drawn in any Psychic Phase, and it goes to the seer of the highest Mastery Level.

A power cast at the tower, or at any Eldar model within 6" of it, is nullified on a D6 roll of 4 or more. An enemy Psyker within 12" that uses a psychic ability or wargear is dragged 2D6" towards the tower, and one that reaches it is drawn through the portal, killed and removed.

Nothing that works through the earth or through matter touches a wraith tower: a Mole Mortar, a Graviton Gun and a Vibrocannon all have no effect. Otherwise it is shot at as any structure is, and read against its own datafax.

Dreadnoughts, sentinels and war walkers are Walkers, and cross terrain as that motive type allows. They carry a Datafax like any vehicle, but with a characteristic profile in place of the usual movement rates. The profile carries no Toughness—that is covered by its armour values.

Their weapons are integrated into the machine's controls, so the occupant may fire any or all of them in the Shooting Phase rather than one weapon per crew member.

Movement

A walker moves under the infantry rules, using the Movement allowance on its profile, and may make a double move to charge or Run, forfeiting its shooting for that turn.

It moves straight ahead in the direction it faces. A free change of facing, up to 90°, is allowed as the move begins and again as it ends; every further turn of up to 90° along the way costs 1".

Close Combat

A machine with a Weapon Skill fights under the normal Hand-to-Hand Combat rules. Unlike other models it may leave close combat freely, brushing man-sized opponents aside. Against a model of its own size it may not, and must fight on.

Crashes & Collisions

A walker steps aside from obstructions as a creature does, so Collisions, Ramming & Overruns does not apply to it. A damaged walker that staggers into a vehicle, a Building or terrain it cannot cross is treated as any other vehicle, and the collision is resolved normally.

A walker damages troops on foot only by attacking them in close combat, and may not overrun them. A model struck by a staggering or falling walker takes damage as normal.

A Space Marine Dreadnought's arms carry variable-configuration weapon mounts, letting it be refitted to suit the tactical situation. The weapons themselves resemble the heavy weapons that Space Marines and Terminators carry, but their mountings are sturdier, feed from deeper magazines, and aim through better targeters. Part of that advantage is already in the Dreadnought's Ballistic Skill and its freedom to move and fire heavy weapons; the rules below carry the rest, and apply to weapons mounted on a Space Marine Dreadnought.

Assault Cannon & Storm Bolter

Jams in a sustained fire weapon come mostly of overheated components or an empty magazine, and the Dreadnought's deep ammo hopper and heavy build hold both at bay. When a Space Marine Dreadnought fires an Assault Cannon or a Storm Bolter, the first Jam rolled on its Sustained Fire Dice each turn is disregarded. A Storm Bolter so mounted therefore never jams, and an Assault Cannon jams only when two or more Jams come up together. Three Jams together still explode the cannon—the weapon is destroyed, and the Dreadnought takes no further harm.

Missile Launcher

Though some older Space Marine Dreadnoughts carry an ordinary Missile Launcher, most mount the salvo-firing Dreadnought Missile Launcher—its rules are given in its own entry.

Multimelta

The Dreadnought's Multimelta carries a variable focus. Fired on a narrow beam it behaves as a standard Multimelta; opened to a broad focus it trades range and power for spread, taking effect as a Heavy Flamer.

Twin Lascannon

The twin Lascannon mount scans a target and picks out its separate components, letting the Dreadnought lay its shot on the piece it wants. Roll to hit as normal. Where a vehicle is hit, the D6 hit location roll is made as usual, and the Space Marine player may then shift it by 1 in either direction. A location behind cover cannot be reached by adjusting the roll.

Power Fist

A Dreadnought Power Fist carries extra servos, gripping a target and rotating to tear pieces away—at its most destructive against vehicles.

The tear attack may only be used against vehicles, Dreadnoughts included. One tear attack may be taken in place of every two hits the Dreadnought would normally score: winning a combat by two allows two ordinary hits or one tear, and a vehicle that would take three hits may instead take one tear and one ordinary hit. To resolve a tear, the Space Marine player nominates a single location on the target and rolls for penetration as normal. Penetrate the chosen location and the piece comes away—damage is rolled at +2 on the damage chart.

Models of one unit stay close together at all times. After a squad moves, a line must be traceable through every model in it, base edge to base edge, with no step longer than 2". Each model is within 2" of the next, not of every other.

Broken Coherency

Over the course of a game a number of scenarios may cause a unit to break Squad Coherency.

During Hand-to-Hand Combat models are not bound by Squad Coherency, but they must return to it once combat has finished.

Casualties are the usual cause, but Squad Coherency may be broken by anything. However it happens, the unit must re-establish coherency in its next Movement Phase. There is no penalty where it can, and where it cannot the smaller part of the split unit counts as being Broken.

That broken part rallies of its own accord the moment coherency is restored, with no Leadership Test asked for.

Dispersed Formation

Certain units fight in Dispersed Formation, which stretches their coherency range to 4".

A vehicle moving over 10" that runs into another vehicle, a Building, or any terrain or Obstacle it cannot cross suffers a collision; where it strikes a vehicle or building, both may take damage. At that speed it may also ram another vehicle deliberately, or overrun troops on foot; both are resolved as collisions.

Collisions Between Vehicles

Each vehicle rolls against the armour of the other. Locations that touch are hit automatically; every other location on both vehicles is hit on a D6 roll of 4+. Armour Penetration is D6 plus the Strength of the vehicle's ram value, plus its damage dice where variable. Compare the total to the Armour Value of each location hit—equal or higher damages that location, so roll a D6 for Damage. Exposed crew that are hit—that is, whose position comes up as a hit location—take a hit at the ram value's Strength, damage and Save Modifier.

Buildings & Terrain

Resolve collisions with buildings and Impassable Terrain the same way: the location that struck first is hit automatically, every other on a 4+. Armour Penetration against a building may not exceed its own Armour Value. The building takes a hit at that same value, which may breach it. Whether other terrain is removed after a collision is left to the players.

Overruns

A vehicle moving 10" or less cannot harm creatures, which have time to step clear. Against a faster vehicle, a creature may dive aside by rolling its Initiative or less on a D6, though a 6 never carries it clear. Those that succeed are placed to either side of the vehicle, unharmed. The second creature a vehicle attempts to overrun in a turn adds +1 to its Initiative, the third +2, and so on. A creature that fails takes a hit at the ram value's Strength, damage and Save Modifier, and the vehicle takes a randomly located hit with a penetration value of that creature's Toughness + D6.

Models which are Stupid must take a Leadership Test at the beginning of their turn. If they pass, they act as normal; however, if they fail, the following rules apply:

  1. If the model is engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat, roll a D6. On a score of 4+, it fights as normal. Otherwise, it forgets what it is doing and stops fighting—it may not roll attack dice or Parry, and only uses Weapon Skill and Combat Score Modifiers when working out the Combat Score.

  2. If the model is not engaged in Hand-to-Hand Combat, a D6 is rolled and read off the chart below:

    Stupid Creature Movement Chart (D6)

    1-3
    Roll a Scatter Dice and move the model its full Movement in the indicated direction. If it encounters an enemy model at any point during this move, it automatically engages them in Hand-to-Hand Combat—but must still roll to see if it fights.
    4+
    The model is so confused it does nothing for the rest of the turn.

  3. The model may not Shoot or use Psychic Powers.

  4. The model is not required to take any other Psychology tests.

While Broken, units are not affected by Stupidity.

If a Cavalry model has a mount which is Stupid, the model has to test for Stupidity but uses the rider's Leadership. A failed test puts the mount under the rules above and takes the rider with it, though the rider fights normally in any combat the mount blunders into. The mount's Attacks are not added to the rider's in a round the mount does not fight.

A Heroic Character leading a Stupid squad moves as the squad moves, but may always fight normally.

A field defence is dug or strung rather than built—a trench, an emplacement, a concealed bunker or a run of razorwire. Each has its own datafax giving its capacity, access, fire arcs, deployment, points and the Armour Value it stands at, and its own damage chart to be read when that armour is beaten. The rules below are common to all four.

Trenches

A trench may be dug to any shape, and joined to others where its ends are left open. A Mole Mortar may be placed in one, and so may a walker or a dreadnought—though neither can leave a trench whose sides stand higher than the model's knee.

Models move along a trench as they would over open ground. Leaving one counts as crossing an Obstacle and costs half the model's Movement; entering costs nothing, so long as there is room to place the model. Crossing a trench likewise counts as moving over an obstacle, and a vehicle treats it as one.

A model charging troops in a trench enters it where there is room, and attacks from the edge where there is not. Attacking from the edge carries the bonus for higher ground. A follow-up move may carry the attacker in.

Models in a trench fire from it under the normal rules, and are fired at under them, with the -2 modifier for Hard Cover.

A Blast Marker is placed as usual. Where its centre hole falls inside the trench, the shot resolves at 1 higher Strength for the enclosed space. Where the centre falls outside but models in the trench lie under the marker, the blast passes over them: each such model rolls a D6, taking a hit on a 4 or more and ducking below the blast untouched on a 1, 2 or 3. A trench is no protection at all against gas.

A trench itself can be attacked only by a Mole Mortar, a Vibrocannon and the Barrage Strategy Card. A Vibrocannon hits automatically and is worked out as it would be against a vehicle, adding 3 to the roll on the trench's own damage chart where it penetrates; the Barrage card penetrates the same armour and rolls on that chart without the modifier. A Mole Mortar uses the chart below in place of its own accuracy chart.

Emplacements

An emplacement is a rampart of earth running up to a wall, with a raised platform behind it, and sections may be joined end to end where their ends are left open.

Models move along an emplacement freely, and enter or leave it at the rear at no cost. Leaving towards the front means crossing the wall, which is an Obstacle costing half the model's Movement, and then the bank, which is difficult ground crossed at half rate.

A charging model therefore reaches the platform only from the foot of the emplacement—a model with a 4" move spends the first half of its charge on the bank and the second crossing the wall. It need not cross at all, but a defender behind the wall then counts it as a defended obstacle. The same costs bind a model using the 4" move of a jump pack to engage. One that leaps the wall to attack from the rear still faces troops standing above it on the platform, and a vehicle treats the whole work as an obstacle.

Models on an emplacement fire under the normal rules and are fired at with the -2 modifier for Hard Cover. A Blast Marker whose centre hole falls behind the wall bursts inside and is resolved as usual; one whose centre falls on or before the wall passes overhead, so every model under the marker rolls a D6, taking a hit on a 4 or more and ducking untouched on a 1, 2 or 3. Gas is unaffected by any of this.

A player attacking the emplacement itself must say so before rolling to hit; a stray blast never harms it. It is a large stationary target, so a shot at Long Range takes +1 To Hit and one at Short Range hits automatically. A shot that penetrates is read on the emplacement's own damage chart.

Concealed Bunkers

A concealed bunker is a small camouflaged dugout. Enough of them must be bought to house a whole squad, and they are not placed on the table at all: a marker goes down instead when field defences deploy, standing for the ground they occupy, and no one marker stands for more than three bunkers. Until they are found the opposing player may do nothing against them.

An enemy unit, character or vehicle that comes within 12" of the marker with Line of Sight to it may test to find them, rolling equal to or under its Initiative on a D6, where a 6 always fails. A unit that Ran that turn adds 1 to the roll and so fails automatically on a 5 or 6, and a squad may test on its leader's Initiative. Occupants that shoot give themselves away without a test.

Once found, place one bunker on the marker and the rest within 4" of it. The troops that found them may fire at them, and the rest of that army may bring weapons with a Blast Marker to bear.

No model may enter a concealed bunker—only those placed in it at the start of the game are ever inside. The occupants may leave in their own Movement Phase at half their Movement, priming a demolition charge that destroys the bunker as they go, and may do nothing else that turn.

Models inside are beyond direct attack, whether or not they fired the turn before, and a shot at the bunker itself takes -1 To Hit. Roll for location and damage as for a vehicle. A weapon with a Blast Marker harms the bunker only on a direct hit, and then damages a single location; one that Scatters onto it does nothing. A bunker may be attacked in Hand-to-Hand Combat as a vehicle is, and a model within 1" of the front may fire or lob a grenade through the Vision Slit at a model inside.

The weapons under Special Weapons reach a bunker's occupants exactly as they reach those of a Fortification, read against the bunker's own armour and its own damage chart.

Razorwire

Razorwire is coiled and torqued so that anything disturbing it lashes back. It counts as Very Difficult Terrain and is crossed at quarter rate. No model may Run through it, and one that runs into it halts at once and moves no further that turn. A vehicle treats it as an Obstacle.

A model whose base lies wholly or partly in razorwire at the end of any Movement Phase takes an automatic Strength 4 hit at -1. It must then roll equal to or under its Initiative on a D6 or be caught in the wire, where a 6 always fails; a model wholly within the wire adds 1 and so fails automatically on a 5 or 6. A caught model does nothing until the end of its next Movement Phase, when it tests again. Models in razorwire may not shoot.

A vehicle crossing razorwire rolls a D6, adding 2 for a ram bar or a bulldozer blade: on a 6 it has torn the wire up, and the razorwire's own damage chart is rolled for.

Only a weapon with a Blast Marker can destroy razorwire. Wire filling the centre hole of the marker is hit automatically, and wire under the marker but not in the hole is hit on a D6 roll of 4 or more. A shot that penetrates is read on that same chart, and models under the marker take the blast as usual.

Some particularly imposing units cause Terror; these units also cause Fear. A squad or Heroic Character model must pass a Leadership Test to overcome their Terror, but they only have to do this once per battle. If they pass, the enemy only causes them Fear from then on. When testing for Terror, a unit does not need to also test for Fear. A unit tests for Terror in the following situations:

  1. The unit is charged by or wants to charge an enemy that causes Terror.

  2. The unit starts its turn within 8" of an enemy that causes Terror.

If a unit fails a Leadership Test for Terror, they are immediately Broken and flee 2D6" straight away from the model that terrified them, even if they are already in cover.

A model that causes Terror is itself beyond the effects of Fear and Terror.

Where such a model leads an ordinary squad, a charge calls for a test only if it will bring the charger into combat with that model itself, and the 8" start-of-turn trigger is measured to that model rather than to the squad it leads.

Cover comes in two kinds: Hard Cover and Soft Cover. When Placing Terrain, players should agree on what terrain provides which kind of cover. Cover conveys a negative To Hit Modifier.

Hard Cover

Features are considered Hard Cover if they can provide a level of solid protection for a model. Examples include walls, ditches, trenches, vehicles, rocks, and the corners of buildings.

A model in a crater, a trench or a pit counts as being in Hard Cover against fire from outside it, wherever within the feature it stands. So does a model placed at the corner or edge of a building, a vehicle or a large rock so that it is partly obscured.

Soft Cover

Features which partially obscure a model, but do not offer substantial protection are considered Soft Cover. Examples include vegetation—hedges, shrubs, woodland, and so on.

The multi-launcher carries ten rockets, fired in programmed salvoes of two. In battles of six or more turns, keep track of ammunition expenditure—in shorter games the launcher will not run dry.

The two rockets of a salvo are primed to detonate together as a single barrage. Set the 3" Blast Marker down and roll to hit as usual. A miss Scatters as usual, with one exception: on a Hit & Misfire result the launcher is not destroyed—a malfunction has occurred instead. Roll a D6 on the chart below.

The firing mechanism fuses. No barrage is fired this turn, but the rockets are expended—mark them off. From then on the launcher fires only after a D6 roll of 4+.

Indirect Fire

A sophisticated scanner suite lets the crew fire on enemies they cannot see. Targets need not be in the firer's Line of Sight, though Choosing a Target otherwise still applies. Set the Blast Marker down and roll to hit as usual; a miss Scatters as ever. Firing Indirectly is less accurate than direct fire: rather than models under the marker being hit automatically, every model—or vehicle location—wholly or partially under the marker is hit on a D6 roll of 4+.

Drach'nyen slides through steel, flesh and bone as though nothing were there, and physical armour is a mockery before it. Every hit wounds automatically and permits no armour saving throw, though unmodifiable saves are taken as normal; a vehicle that is struck has its armour penetrated automatically. Psykers and daemons suffer D3 wounds from a hit instead of 1.

Heavy—the quad launcher moves only under its own power, up to 4" in the Movement Phase while a crew member is within the 4" reach of its radio control box. It cannot cross difficult terrain or obstacles, pivots freely on the spot, and otherwise moves only under tow behind a vehicle; readying it to shoot means it cannot move and fire in one turn.

Gun and crew are separate targets—shots at short range may pick the gun or either crew member, long-range hits randomise—and one of its two crew runs it alone, though with both dead it stands idle. The gun takes fire at an Armour Value of 10, a penetrating hit wrecking it; crew who lose it fight on alone, reinforce another thudd gun, or take over one left crewless.

Each shot is a salvo of four bursts laid out with the special Thudd Gun Salvo template. Fire at a visible target as with any weapon—roll to hit, Scatter on a miss—then:

  1. Centre burst 1 on the landing point, arrow pointing straight back at the gun.

  2. Roll a D12; set blast 2's arrow to that number on blast 1's rim. Place blasts 3 and 4 the same way, each from the one before.

  3. A model wholly under any template is hit, partly under on a D6 roll of 4+—one hit at most, however many templates cover it.

Speculative fire drops a salvo where the crew cannot see:

  1. Declare in the Shooting Phase and mark any point within maximum range; aligning the gun takes the whole turn, so it does not shoot.

  2. It must stay put through the enemy turn and its own next Movement Phase—moving removes the marker and restarts the process.

  3. In its next Shooting Phase it may fire at the mark: roll to hit as normal, scatter misses, lay the template as above.

Place the template touching the firing model's base. The template moves straight forward—any models that the template moves over are hit. Partially covered models are hit on a D6 roll of 4+. The template stops if it hits a vehicle, building, or other substantial obstacle, but passes through woods, hills, and low walls.

The attack begins at S7, but is reduced by 1 for every 3" travelled—once it reaches S0 it is removed. The Save Modifier is equal to half the current Strength, rounded down. Armour Penetration against vehicles is equal to Strength at point of impact + D6.

The Doom Siren does not encumber its user, who may also carry Basic weapons. However, it cannot be used in Hand-to-Hand Combat or in addition to shooting with another weapon.

The Neural Shredder is fired at the end of the Imperial player's Hand-to-Hand Combat phase, and only while no enemy model stands in base-to-base contact with the Callidus Assassin. Place the Flamer template with its point touching the Assassin: models wholly beneath it are hit automatically, and a model partly beneath it is hit if a D6 scores 4 or better.

A hit burns the mind, not the body. Every model hit takes a Leadership test at -2 to its Leadership. Failure costs 1 wound with a -3 Save Modifier—and armour fields give no protection at all.

A serum is chosen before rolling to hit. If the target's armour or field saving throw fails, the serum takes hold automatically—no roll to wound is made. Serums affect only living creatures; against anything else the needler falls back on its basic profile.

Xyclos A deals D3 wounds per hit, automatically. Xyclos B breeds psychotic visions—a D6+2 roll on the Hallucinogen Effect Chart decides which. Xyclos C sets the target alight as though ignited by a flamer; the flames cannot be smothered, though they may burn out on their own, and a model that dies explodes with the effects of a Plasma Grenade.

A model armed with a Power Scourge gains +2 Attacks. Hits are resolved at the wielder's Strength. The Scourge is impossible to Parry. Additionally, multiple combatants do not gain their normal bonuses (+1 combat resolution and extra Attack Dice).

The cannon fires ordinary ammunition or Shrieker ammunition on the same profile—the Shrieker rules are in the rulebook. So fine is its making that any Jam rolled on the Sustained Fire Dice is ignored. The Maugetar needs both hands, and cannot parry.

Its crew member directs it from up to 4" away by control box. It moves up to 4" in the Movement Phase, only under its own power and never through difficult terrain or over obstacles; it may move and fire in the same turn, and fires in any direction.

Platform and crew member are separate targets—the firer picks at short range where both are visible, randomises at long—and the platform takes fire as a vehicle with an Armour Value of 10: penetration destroys it outright, while a dead crew member leaves it standing idle. A crew member who loses the platform fights on alone, reinforces another Tarantula, or takes over one left crewless.
A stripped-down laser weapon that trades the reach and punch of the heavier patterns for lightness and a faster recharge—so unlike them, it may be fired on the move.

The lasblaster fires three shots each Shooting phase, rolling to hit each separately; every target must lie within 6" of the others. The powered blade fixed to its stock fights with the second profile.

When the Psychic phase ends, up to two unspent force cards may be laid into the blade rather than discarded, and drawn out again in later Psychic phases. In Hand-to-Hand Combat it adds the wielder's Mastery Level to their Strength, and it wounds daemons outright, no saving throw permitted. Stored cards may be expended for more: each one spent is worth a further +2 Strength and -2 on the armour save. The blade parries.

When the Psychic phase ends, up to two unspent force cards may be laid into the spear rather than discarded, and drawn out again in later Psychic phases. It may be thrown up to 12" in the Shooting phase, returning to the psyker afterwards. Thrown or swung, it adds the wielder's Mastery Level to their Strength and wounds daemons outright, no saving throw permitted; each stored force card expended is worth a further +2 Strength and -2 on the armour save.
A power weapon needing both hands, whatever shape it takes. It parries.

The sword may be swung in one hand or both—choose each time it attacks, using the matching profile: a hand free to fight with a second weapon, or a single devastating blow. Charged with the psychic power of Asurmen, its wounds ignore daemonic saving throws entirely.

To fire this weapon, place the Medium Flamer Template so that its pointed end touches the firing model. Unlike normal template weapons, the Spinefist must roll to hit—make a To Hit roll against every target at least half under the template, applying normal modifiers for cover and target movement.

In Hand-to-Hand Combat the template is not used—at such close quarters the target absorbs all of the spines before they start to fan out.

The Thunder Hammer is so powerful that its Strength value is not recorded. Models hit by it are automatically wounded—though they may still make Armour Saves. Against vehicles, the hull is automatically penetrated by the blow.
Gives a Basic weapon a close combat option. The entry stands for every blade or saw fixed to a Basic Weapon, whatever its shape.

Heavy—can move a maximum of 2" per turn.

Of its crew of two, one is enough to fire it. The other serves as forward observer—the spotter—free to leave the weapon and its operator, linked back to both, letting the mortar be fired at a point the spotter sees but the firer cannot. If the firer is killed, the spotter may return and take the weapon over.

This weapon cannot target a point within 12" of itself; however, the shot may Scatter to within this distance. It can target any other point on the tabletop that is in Line of Sight of at least one crew member.

The Scorpion's Bite shoots automatically before close combat is resolved, exactly as a mandiblaster does—work the shot out as normal shooting. On a hit, roll two D6 and keep the higher: if the score equals or beats the target's Toughness, the target takes D3 wounds, saving at -3.
Light enough to wield at blurring speed: its bearer may Parry twice in each round of Hand-to-Hand Combat.

Thrown, it hunts. Nominate the first target and roll to hit; on a hit, nominate another target within 2" of the last and roll again, and so on until a miss, or until no further target lies in range and within 2" of the previous one. The weapon then returns to the thrower's hand of its own accord.

Cast like a spinning bolas, it may be sent at three targets, no two of them more than 12" apart, striking one after another before returning to its wielder's hand. In Hand-to-Hand Combat it swings as a flail on the same Strength and Save Modifier.
Not built for fighting, but it serves. A living opponent who loses even one wound to the Blades is left helpless by the pain: the model is removed as a casualty, whatever wounds it still has.
The pistol needs a few seconds to recharge between shots. In hand-to-hand combat only the first hit landed in each round can be struck with it; every hit after that is dealt with Dante's power axe.
A potent close combat weapon, and one that can be turned to parry.

Worn as a pair, the gauntlets grant an extra attack dice in close combat, and let the wearer meet many opponents at once—enemies gain no multiple combat bonuses against him. The built-in boltguns fire together with the effect of a single storm bolter.
Once per Hand-to-Hand Combat phase, as it opens, the Bale Eye automatically hits any one model already locked in combat with Yarrick.

A creature hit falls under Stupidity at once. At the start of each following turn it takes a normal Leadership test: a failure prolongs the effect, a pass shakes it off entirely and no further tests are needed.

Lay the Large Flamer Template with its tip against the cannon and its length pointing at the target. Roll an Artillery Dice and push the template that many inches forward; a Misfire leaves it where it is.

Anything the template passes over on its way—Misfire included—is hit on a D6 roll of 4+, and anything wholly beneath it is hit automatically.

A model hit and killed is removed. One that is hit and lives rolls on the Inferno Cannon Hit Table:

1-3
The target does not catch—what little chemical fuel landed on it burns out at once.
4+

A target that Ignites Catches On Fire.

The Inferno Cannon counts as a Flamer Weapon for special rules and invulnerabilities.

A shrunken head taken from a victim of one of Nurgle's favourite plagues, packed with virulent pus and infected biting flies and stoppered with wax. Thrown, it bursts over the target in a noisome cloud of flies and corruption.

Thrown under the ordinary grenade rules, and may be aimed at a patch of ground like Smoke or Blind grenades. Set a Blight marker where it lands. Every model within 2" of the marker is hit; one only partly within that reach is hit on a D6 roll of 4, 5 or 6. Each hit has a Strength of D6, rolled separately for every target, and inflicts 1 wound. Should any Strength roll come up 1 the Blight has thinned to a mere nuisance: resolve that S1 hit, then lift the marker—everyone else beneath it has had a lucky escape.

Armour saves are taken as normal and unmodified, but sealed suits are no sure defence—flies clog breathers, pus creeps into joints and eyepieces—so no saving throw for an energy field or a dodge may be taken. Open-topped vehicle crews are affected like foot troops. For an enclosed vehicle within reach roll a D6: on a 6 the Blight finds its way in and each crew member takes a hit, Strength rolled as above. Dreadnoughts and robots are wholly unaffected, as are Nurgle daemons and any Chaos model bearing the Mark of Nurgle.

A marker left in place goes on infecting: it hits anything that moves within 2" of it in later turns, and a model already affected that fails to move clear of it in its next Movement phase takes a further hit, Strength rolled again.

On a miss, roll a Sustained Fire Dice to determine the number of 1" Blast Markers to Scatter away from the target. Should any template come up Hit/Misfire, the coils go: a Catastrophic Coil Burnout.

A Jam on any Sustained Fire Dice silences the weapon for that turn and the next, as though it were recharging. Fired at Maximum Power, though, a Jam brings the burnout on at once:

Roll at once on the damage table for the arm carrying the gun. Everything within D3" takes an S5 hit at -2 save modifier.
4+
Everything within D3" takes an S5 hit at -2 save modifier, and the weapon is left Jammed.

A power sword in all respects but one: the long, curved blade is made for the saddle, and its potency rises with the jetbike's momentum. Use the profile matching the rider's current speed—at full tilt the blade is nothing but a streak of electric blue light.

Carried by Space Marine Dreadnoughts. Each turn it may fire a single missile, or salvo fire—declare which before rolling to hit. To salvo fire, roll a Sustained Fire Dice and launch that many missiles of a single type, rolling to hit for each separately; missiles may be fired at different targets no more than 2" apart.

If a Jam is rolled, no missiles are fired and the launcher Jams like any sustained fire weapon: it must miss its shot in the next Shooting Phase while the jam is cleared. The model's other weapons are unaffected.

Adds 3 to any roll made on a Datafax damage table; a modified result above 6 is read as 6.

Firing it requires the vehicle to have stood still that turn—the rest of its weapons are unaffected.

The pairing is fixed before the game and either written down or declared to the opponent. Two boltguns count as a Storm Bolter.

In each Shooting Phase the bearer either fires one barrel, resolved exactly as that weapon normally is, or fires both at a single target at a further -1 to hit on each shot.
Roll the Artillery Dice for Strength every time the shoota fires—anything from 2 to 10. A Misfire means the shoota has exploded: the weapon is destroyed and the Ork holding it takes a Strength 4 hit.

Roll the Artillery Dice for Strength each time the blasta fires—anything from 2 to 10—and roll for the size of its blast marker too, a D3" radius. A Misfire means the blasta has exploded: the weapon is destroyed and the Ork holding it takes a Strength 4 hit.

If the shot hits, the target is lifted into the air. Roll a D6: the crew may move the victim up to that many inches before dropping it. Roll the Scatter Dice to determine which direction the model faces when it lands.

Dropped foot troopers and Terminators suffer 1 wound with a -1 save modifier. A dropped vehicle takes damage as if it had collided with a building: its legs, wheels or tracks take damage at the vehicle's own ram value, with every other location doing the same on a D6 roll of 4+. Dropped support weapons are destroyed.

Anything under the victim when it is dropped takes damage as a collision, using the dropped model's ram values—it always counts as having been moving 10" or more, however far it was actually moved. A large vehicle may land on several models; work out damage against each separately. Foot models get no chance to dodge, and a dropped model takes no additional damage for landing on another.

A Nemesis Force Weapon is made for daemon hunting and carries a storm bolter in its haft. When the Psychic Phase ends, unused Force Cards—up to two at once—may be kept in the blade instead of being discarded, ready for later psychic phases.

In Hand-to-Hand Combat the weapon raises the wielder's Strength by their Mastery Level; daemons are wounded automatically, with no saving throw allowed. A stored Force Card may be expended as it strikes a daemon to deepen the wound: one card for D3 wounds, two for D6.
Thrown exactly as a grenade. Where the clay pot breaks, place a Buzzer Squig template and work out the swarm exactly like a Squig Katapult attack landing on the spot.

The staff is a force weapon: in Hand-to-Hand Combat the Weirdboy adds their Mastery Level to their Strength, and daemons are wounded outright. Carrying it also lets the Weirdboy reroll a failed Waaagh! test, once.

A model that loses even a single wound to the Rod is overwhelmed: it comes off the table as a casualty, however many wounds it still has. The victim must also pass a Leadership test on 2D6 or die screaming, so horribly that a Break test is forced on every friendly model within 8".

The beamer moves only under its own power: as far as 4" in the Movement Phase, provided a crew member stays inside 4"—the reach of its radio control. Difficult terrain and obstacles bar it, and a turn spent moving is a turn it cannot fire. Facing can be changed freely at any moment, and a vehicle may tow it.

The weapon and its crew are separate targets: at short range an attacker picks either; at long range, randomise. One crew member dead, the weapon still moves and fires; both dead, it stands on the table useless. Its Armour Value is 10, treated as a vehicle's—penetration destroys it outright. Crew left alive may fight on alone, crew a different support weapon that has lost its own, or attach themselves to another as spares.

Roll to hit as normal, applying a penalty based on the target's maximum movement:

It may be fired only in a turn the vehicle has not moved—its other weapons fire as usual. Shots must fall within a 45° forward arc.

The Earthshaker fires two shells at a single target. Roll to hit for each shell separately; shells that miss Scatter as normal. Damage is worked out shell by shell—where both land, targets under the 2" Blast Marker are struck twice and roll damage for each.

Against any target that uses a Datafax, location and armour penetration are rolled as for any other hit. A penetrating hit rolls a D6 on the location's damage table; a hit that fails to penetrate still rolls a D3 on the damage table.

A model charged by a Howling Banshee wearing the mask may not fire Overwatch at the charge, and must hold its ground. In the first round of the combat that follows it rolls no Attack Dice.

The mask works on the Banshee's own charge alone, and does nothing where the Howling Banshee is itself charged. Its effect is spent after that first round.

The target may be a model, a piece of scenery, or any visible patch of ground. Everything under the marker is caught in the loop; a model only partly under it is caught on a D6 roll of 4, 5 or 6, and is otherwise moved clear.

Inside the loop nothing happens at all. Trapped models may not act, and nothing outside can affect them—they cannot move, shoot, or be shot at. A loop cannot be shot through, though it can be seen through normally.

Such models move at half rate in their own turn, and may shoot or use Psychic Powers only if a D6 first scores 4 or more. Hand-to-Hand Combat is fought every other turn.

Firing into the distortion, out of it, or clean through it, carries -2 To Hit. A model with the movement to leave the distortion is free of it; one that moves from the distortion into the loop is trapped.

Hits are worked out as for any Hand-to-Hand Combat. A model that is hit takes an immediate armour saving throw; a save that is passed leaves it unharmed, and one that fails kills it outright.

Against a dreadnought or a vehicle the wire does no damage unless it reaches the crew, and it carries its own Armour Penetration. Roll a D6: a score of 1 to 5 is the number of points penetrated. A 6 is rolled again and added, and again for as long as 6s follow.

The Mandiblaster fires before the combat proper is worked out, and is resolved as ordinary Shooting. A hit calls for a D6: a score equal to or above the target's Toughness inflicts a single wound.

Once Hand-to-Hand Combat is under way the Mandiblaster has no further effect, and a model carrying one rolls no extra Attack Dice for it.

A launcher strapped to the leg of an Eldar Swooping Hawk, which releases grenades downward as the warrior flies over. It takes Frag and Krak Grenades only, and carries enough of both to last the battle.

While in flight the model may drop one grenade anywhere directly beneath its flight path. Dropped grenades are worked out in the Movement Phase, rolling To Hit and scattering as a thrown grenade does.

Dropping a grenade does not stop the model firing in the Shooting Phase, though it may not drop a grenade and throw one in the same turn. Single grenades may also be taken from the pack and thrown by hand.
Talons that shear through armour plate at the bearer's own Strength. Heavier creatures cut deeper, so the two profiles differ only in save modifier.

The Plasma Blaster is a combi-weapon developed after the Storm Bolter. The bulk of the power packs it requires means only models in Terminator Armour may use one.

It is not a linked weapon and may not be fired as a single Plasma Gun. It takes a turn to recharge, as an ordinary plasma gun does.
A master-crafted plasma pistol draws on a far better energy source than the ordinary Plasma Pistol: it needs no turn to recharge after firing, and may fire every turn.

The Wailing Doom is no mortal weapon but the manifestation of a dark and sinister god—a part of the Avatar imbued with its power. Daemons attacked by the Wailing Doom do not get their Daemonic saving throw

The lance tip explodes on impact during the first round of Hand-to-Hand Combat—afterwards the lance is discarded, even if the attacker missed. Charging lancers receive a +2 Combat Score for the first round only; this bonus does not apply if charged.
The blade runs with virulent slime. Each wound it deals a living creature calls for a D6—a 6 kills the victim outright.
The blade runs with venomous slime. Each Wound it deals a living creature calls for a D6—a 4+ kills the victim outright.
A model hit and not killed recoils from the fire, moving to whichever edge of the template is closest.

Roll to hit as usual; a miss rolls to Scatter. The seed pod deals an S4 hit at -1 save modifier, and anything it wounds dies outright. Centre a 3" Blast Marker on the body.

Every model and every vehicle even partly beneath the template rolls a D6. On 1-3 it gets clear and acts normally next turn. On 4+ the barbs have it: roll 2D6 against its Strength—or its Ram Value, for a vehicle—and a higher score means dead or held fast for good, counting as destroyed. Anything less and it tears loose to act normally next turn, a vehicle doing so Out of Control.
A squad that loses even one model to a Blastmaster takes a Break Test.

May be fired alongside another weapon, so the model shoots twice in a turn. One type of Grenade is loaded before the game and that is what it fires; there is no reloading once play starts. Strength, Damage, Save Modifier and Armour Penetration all come from the grenade loaded.

Digilasers hide in finger rings, or along the knuckles of a glove, and leave the model free to use any other weapon.

The moment Hand-to-Hand Combat begins they fire of their own accord—before any attack dice are rolled, whichever side's turn it is—at opponents in base contact. The shots—three, divided between opponents as the model wishes—are worked out as ordinary shooting.

Once close combat proper is under way the digilasers do nothing further, and grant no extra attack dice.

The psycannon exists to hurt Psykers and daemons; its workings come from the Storm Bolter, its bolts steeped in psychic energy.

Its bolts wound a daemon or a Psyker without a roll, and a daemon gets no saving throw at all. Any Psyker or daemon it damages loses one Psychic Power, chosen at random, for the rest of the battle.

A suit of Terminator Armour may be fitted with a harness of auto-launchers similar to those mounted on vehicles. The harness carries three grenades of the same type, fired together, and may be triggered in addition to the model's normal firing.

One grenade strikes a point exactly 6" away within the model's 90° fire arc; the other two land D3" off that point. Before battle the harness is loaded with either Frag or Blind grenades.

A Force Axe spits and crackles with barely contained psychic charge. When the Psychic Phase ends, one unused Force Card may be kept in the axe instead of being discarded, ready for a later psychic phase.

In Hand-to-Hand Combat the axe raises the wielder's Strength by their Mastery Level; daemons are wounded automatically, with no saving throw allowed. The stored Force Card may be expended for a further +3 Strength and a -3 save modifier in that combat.

A Force Rod's helix-shaped core drinks in psychic energy, and holds more of it than any blade. When the Psychic Phase ends, unused Force Cards—up to three at once—may be kept in the rod instead of being discarded, ready for later psychic phases.

In Hand-to-Hand Combat the rod raises the wielder's Strength by their Mastery Level; daemons are wounded automatically, with no saving throw allowed.

Thrown with a 2" blast marker, scattering like any other grenade, and doing the damage of a Frag Grenade where it lands.

Its real work is on Psykers. Any caught wholly or partly beneath the marker lose the use of their powers until the turn ends, anything they already have running is nullified on the spot, and force cards held in a weapon or similar device are discarded. Supply is short: roll a D6 after each throw, and on a 1 or 2 there are none left for the battle.

May fire three shell types—the player must declare which shell is being used before declaring a target.

The player may opt to fire directly at any target that is within the Heavy Mortar's Firing Arc and the crew's Line of Sight. When firing directly, the Choosing a Target rule still applies and the player must still roll on the Guess Range Scatter Chart.
Adds 2 to the wielder's Strength for the opening round of combat and nothing thereafter. A flail cannot be parried. Chains, morning stars and their kin are all covered here.
Every model within 2" of the one struck rolls a D6, and is caught on a 4+. Being caught means an S3 hit at no saving throw modifier.

Thrown rather than swung. How far it reaches is worked out from the thrower's Strength, the way a grenade's is, and the attack is resolved like any other Shooting attack. A homing mechanism carries the blade back to its owner once it has struck.
The blade slips in and out of real space as it moves, so armour is simply not there when it lands. Nothing wounded by it gets an armour saving throw, and an armour field is no help either.
Two weapons in one housing. The firer picks a barrel each time they shoot and may never use both in a single shot, though a model with Fast Shot may divide a turn's shots between the two.

Injectors set in the fingers deliver acids and nerve toxins, and only living things are troubled by them. A squad that loses anyone to the glove must test to break at once.

A victim wounded but left alive has every characteristic halved for the rest of the battle, fractions rounded up, whatever Wounds it has left included. The temple reworks the mixture constantly, so Tyranids are no more resistant than anyone else; daemons, having nothing to poison, are unaffected.

Fires through the Heavy Flamer Template, and everything even partly beneath it is a target.

Roll 1D6 per target: a score above the model's Initiative hits, a 6 always hits, and add 1 where the template covers the model entirely. Anything that dodges the cloud is placed at the nearest point on the template's outer edge.

A model caught in the cloud is pinned for the remainder of the Shooting Phase and is hit automatically by any further Death Spinner fire. Failing its Armour Save kills it outright.

A vehicle location under the template, wholly or in part, is hit on a D6 roll of 4+; exposed crew beneath it are hit automatically. Armour Penetration is D6, and every 6 rolled adds another D6, on and on until something other than a 6 comes up. A penetrating hit is resolved on the chart below:

A model that cannot see through the cloud may not shoot into or through it. Psychic powers cross smoke unhindered, though a psyker still cannot see through it unaided.

A model inside the cloud either stands still or moves at half rate in a direction rolled at random. One fighting in Hand-to-Hand Combat inside it does so at half Weapon Skill, rounding up.

Radiation cannot be seen, and a scanner is the only thing that reads it—which few troopers carry.
